The point of the QBI program is not to pay the private sector to develop the tech, which they’re already doing on their own, according to program manager Joe Altepeter. Instead, in essence, a company that wins a QBI award gets access to DARPA’s interagency team of expert testers and devil’s advocates, serving as an independent outside check to make sure that they’re on a practical path.

Tech titan Microsoft and specialist startup PsiQuantum have already won contracts for the initial, pilot-project version of the program, known clunkily as Underexplored Systems for Utility-Scale Quantum Computing or US2QC . (“You can tell why we changed it to ‘QBI,’” Altepeter said). Two other companies, Atom Computing and QC82 , also won preliminary, short-term grants in 2023, but their proposals didn’t survive subsequent rounds of more intensive scrutiny. So only two of four competing firms made it all the way through the three-phase process to win one of the long-term “Stage C” contracts announced Feb. 6.
That 50 percent success rate is actually much better than Altepeter expected.
“That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C. But that’s why we do this, to get surprised.”

So a “major expansion” to “bring in many more companies” is now underway, Altepeter said. “We’ve gotten finished with source selection [and] sent out letters inviting all the companies who’ve made it into stage A to negotiate a contract…. My best guess is late March, we’re going to have the vast majority of those contracts signed.”

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers. As a result, “we’ll have the chance to kick the tires on a lot more companies,” he said. “A year from now, we’ll know a lot more about if this industry is for real or not.”

How does that timeline work? The process is meant to be flexible, with the schedule accommodating what companies think is required, and companies that fail at one stage of the evaluation — like Atom and QC82 — are welcome to come back for a second shot. But overall, Altepeter said, QBI goes like this:

At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said. Currently, it consists of roughly 200 quantum experts from across the government — including Energy Department labs like Los Alamos as well as Defense Department labs like the Air Force Research Laboratory — and government-funded research centers, such as Johns Hopkins. (These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work). The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way.

With new technologies, it’s all too easy to get sucked in by hype cycles and impressive statistics, Altepeter said, so it’s critical, and difficult, to figure out the right way to measure progress. Track the wrong metrics, he warned, and you end up with the equivalent of assessing a space-launch program by highest altitude achieved to date, a superficially reasonable approach that ends up grading grifters who can climb a ladder over professionals conducting static rocket-motor tests.
“We are building by far the best, largest test and evaluation team for quantum computing on the planet,” Altepeter summed up. “[We’re] planning for this to be a $1 billion-plus program.”
This kind of careful evaluation isn’t cheap, he acknowledged, and if too many companies prove qualified, he may not have enough funding to give all of them awards.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” Altepeter said. “I’m pleasantly surprised that these companies were doing so well. I also worry that we couldn’t eliminate as many companies, because we’re definitely trying to eliminate companies.”

Could the Trump Administration’s controversial ongoing cuts to government agencies, spearheaded by Elon Musk’s DOGE , cramp or cripple the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative just as it’s trying to grow? Altepeter demurred on those “bigger-scope…budget issues.”

sources.title: The world needs ever faster data processing. Edge computing will help - Mastercard
passages: The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever.
Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate.
Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data.
The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection.
This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through.

For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves.
That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again.
The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second.
For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world.
In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols.
Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately.
Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center.

Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes.
The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds.
Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers.
The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones.
As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage.
Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster.
And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously.
It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway.
Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions.
There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations.
Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

extraction.body: Few innovations have transformed our relationship with technology like the cloud. This constellation of huge data centers can tackle computing tasks for digital devices located a mile or a continent away, allowing us to enjoy podcasts, share memes or stream movies nearly anywhere we go. The cloud, however, has a problem. It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway. That means more and more data and computing is being shuttled back and forth across the cloud’s connections, and more is coming. Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions. There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations. Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center. Edge computing isn’t new. Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes. Two technological shifts are behind this push to make more use of the network edge. The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds. Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers. The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones. For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world. In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols. Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately. Those days are over. As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage. Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster. The solution is to constantly evolve the network to make the edge do more work. Mastercard’s global network, for example, processes tens of billions of transactions a year, linking merchants, banks, government agencies, fintechs and open banking networks. The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection. This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through. Public cloud and 5G have increased consumer expectations for speed in our digital interactions, but they also allow for a range of innovations. For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves. That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again. The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second. Any longer and lines would start to stretch. There are applications, though, with even lower tolerances for lag. Congestion pricing is being used by more cities as a way to discourage drivers from bringing their vehicles into city centers during rush hour. And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously. The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever. Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate. Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data. Someday soon, we won’t just use our phones or wallets for commerce. Cars and kitchen appliances will play a role, too — recommending when it’s time for new tires, an oil change or a gallon of milk. Managing all that data and creating a unified experience across all of these devices will be a huge challenge. Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has become a major beneficiary of rising demand for memory chips, which has fueled record revenue and earnings growth over the last year. What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory. If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models . As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market. One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate. Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers. SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems. Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has become a major beneficiary of rising demand for memory chips, which has fueled record revenue and earnings growth over the last year. What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory. If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models . As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market. One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate. Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers. SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems. Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic are all developing custom silicon chips. This provides yet another tailwind for increased memory demand and could help SK Hynix diversify across different AI computing architectures. In other words, SK Hynix doesn't need one chip designer to dominate the AI infrastructure era indefinitely. It simply needs advanced memory to remain essential to the broader AI ecosystem. While AI-driven growth has fueled substantial earnings expansion for SK Hynix, the company's valuation remains fairly modest on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis. The company's leadership in the HBM market and progress in new chip technology give SK Hynix strong competitive advantages that extend beyond today's memory supercycle. When combined with its attractive valuation profile, I view SK Hynix as a compelling long-term buy for investors seeking exposure to the AI infrastructure boom. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $2,783,470 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. *Stock Advisor returns as of October 18, 2026. Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has become a major beneficiary of rising demand for memory chips, which has fueled record revenue and earnings growth over the last year. What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory.
If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models .

As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out.

According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market.

One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate.

Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers.

SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems.

Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic are all developing custom silicon chips. This provides yet another tailwind for increased memory demand and could help SK Hynix diversify across different AI computing architectures. In other words, SK Hynix doesn't need one chip designer to dominate the AI infrastructure era indefinitely. It simply needs advanced memory to remain essential to the broader AI ecosystem.
While AI-driven growth has fueled substantial earnings expansion for SK Hynix, the company's valuation remains fairly modest on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis.

The company's leadership in the HBM market and progress in new chip technology give SK Hynix strong competitive advantages that extend beyond today's memory supercycle. When combined with its attractive valuation profile, I view SK Hynix as a compelling long-term buy for investors seeking exposure to the AI infrastructure boom.

Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

sources.title: MARA-Linked Wallets Send 1,000 BTC to Binance & Gate: Is the Bitcoin Miner Selling Again? - The Crypto Times
passages: Wallets linked to MARA Holdings, one of the largest publicly listed bitcoin mining companies, have deposited 1,000 Bitcoin (BTC) , worth around about $82.8 million at current prices, into crypto exchanges Binance and Gate over the past five days, according to on-chain data from blockchain analytics firm Lookonchain.
MARA-linked wallets moved 1,996 BTC to Binance, Gate, and Galaxy Digital in October, as its latest filing outlines plans for opportunistic Bitcoin sales.
The deposits follow another large movement earlier in October.

Around October 8 and 9, 2026, a wallet labeled “MARA Miner” moved 996.105 BTC, then worth about $81.13 million, to an address associated with Galaxy Digital, a digital asset financial services and investment firm.
Blockchain records confirmed that transfer but did not show whether the coins were later sold.

In the letter, MARA said it historically held the Bitcoin it produced as a long-term investment, began selling in 2025 to fund operations, and expects to keep selling Bitcoin opportunistically during 2026 to provide liquidity or fund capital projects, depending on market conditions.
During Q2, MARA mined 2,422 BTC, sold 2,213 BTC at an average price of $73,078, and bought no Bitcoin, the same filing shows.
The quarter followed a heavier round of disposals earlier in the year, when MARA sold nearly $1 billion worth of Bitcoin to cut its debt by about 30%.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) , the company held 35,577 BTC as of June 30, 2026.
That total included 9,270 BTC that were loaned out or pledged as collateral, and it marked a 29% decline from a year earlier.
Lookonchain, which tracks large wallet movements on public blockchains, reported the transfers on October 19, 2026, and said the activity appeared consistent with possible selling.
That approach has set MARA apart from corporate bitcoin holders such as Strive that continue to accumulate.
MARA Holdings, Inc. ( NASDAQ : MARA), formerly known as Marathon Digital Holdings, has not issued a public statement on the deposits at the time of writing.

passages: Wallets linked to MARA Holdings, one of the largest publicly listed bitcoin mining companies, have deposited 1,000 Bitcoin (BTC) , worth around about $82.8 million at current prices, into crypto exchanges Binance and Gate over the past five days, according to on-chain data from blockchain analytics firm Lookonchain.
MARA-linked wallets moved 1,996 BTC to Binance, Gate, and Galaxy Digital in October, as its latest filing outlines plans for opportunistic Bitcoin sales.
The deposits follow another large movement earlier in October.

Around October 8 and 9, 2026, a wallet labeled “MARA Miner” moved 996.105 BTC, then worth about $81.13 million, to an address associated with Galaxy Digital, a digital asset financial services and investment firm.
Blockchain records confirmed that transfer but did not show whether the coins were later sold.

During Q2, MARA mined 2,422 BTC, sold 2,213 BTC at an average price of $73,078, and bought no Bitcoin, the same filing shows.
The quarter followed a heavier round of disposals earlier in the year, when MARA sold nearly $1 billion worth of Bitcoin to cut its debt by about 30%.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) , the company held 35,577 BTC as of June 30, 2026.
That total included 9,270 BTC that were loaned out or pledged as collateral, and it marked a 29% decline from a year earlier.
Lookonchain, which tracks large wallet movements on public blockchains, reported the transfers on October 19, 2026, and said the activity appeared consistent with possible selling.
That approach has set MARA apart from corporate bitcoin holders such as Strive that continue to accumulate.
MARA Holdings, Inc. ( NASDAQ : MARA), formerly known as Marathon Digital Holdings, has not issued a public statement on the deposits at the time of writing.

In the letter, MARA said it historically held the Bitcoin it produced as a long-term investment, began selling in 2025 to fund operations, and expects to keep selling Bitcoin opportunistically during 2026 to provide liquidity or fund capital projects, depending on market conditions.
During Q2, MARA mined 2,422 BTC, sold 2,213 BTC at an average price of $73,078, and bought no Bitcoin, the same filing shows.
The quarter followed a heavier round of disposals earlier in the year, when MARA sold nearly $1 billion worth of Bitcoin to cut its debt by about 30%.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) , the company held 35,577 BTC as of June 30, 2026.
That total included 9,270 BTC that were loaned out or pledged as collateral, and it marked a 29% decline from a year earlier.
Lookonchain, which tracks large wallet movements on public blockchains, reported the transfers on October 19, 2026, and said the activity appeared consistent with possible selling.
That approach has set MARA apart from corporate bitcoin holders such as Strive that continue to accumulate.
MARA Holdings, Inc. ( NASDAQ : MARA), formerly known as Marathon Digital Holdings, has not issued a public statement on the deposits at the time of writing.

extraction.body: The artificial intelligence boom began with the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. The viral application brought generative AI into the mainstream, setting in motion a sequence of events that has led to one of the most aggressive investment cycles in history. To date, the AI trade has largely focused on semiconductor companies and infrastructure providers, but Morgan Stanley analysts think we've reached an inflection point where the AI trade will broaden to software companies and AI adopters, meaning businesses that use the technology to reduce costs. Here are two stocks Morgan Stanley analysts believe are well-positioned to benefit as the AI trade evolves. The next wave of the artificial intelligence boom "will likely reward companies that use the technology to improve decisions, lower costs, and strengthen margins -- not just those building AI infrastructure," according to Ellen Zenter, strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management. Amazon ( AMZN -1.87% ) is an excellent example. The company is leveraging expertise in artificial intelligence and robotics to make its retail business more efficient. Amazon has developed dozens of generative AI applications that optimize inventory management, last-mile delivery, and warehouse operations. The company has also developed AI models that make its robots faster and more productive. While costly, investments in those areas have already moved the needle. Amazon's trailing-12-month operating margin expanded more than 3 percentage points in the last two years, reaching 12.1% in the most recent quarter. Operating income increased at 21% annually over the same period. But the company still has room to reduce costs. Morgan Stanley analysts led by Brian Nowak view Amazon as the most underappreciated beneficiary of generative AI across their coverage universe, and they expect the company's operating margin to hit 17% by 2028 as retail operations become increasingly efficient. "We're expanding our deployment of robotics and automation, which have been integral to our operations for decades," CFO Brian Olsavsky told analysts. He also said the company will more than double its fleet of robotic arms this year. "We see meaningful opportunities to further enhance productivity across our global fulfillment network." Wall Street expects earnings to grow at 21% annually over the next three years, but that figure could be low. Amazon beat the consensus earnings estimate in five of the last six quarters, and it may continue to do so as AI and robotics drive efficiency gains. That makes the current valuation of 20 times earnings look downright cheap. Morgan Stanley analysts led by Stephen Byrd still see upside in semiconductor stocks like Nvidia and Broadcom , but they also expect the AI trade to broaden to software companies. sources.title: Autel Achieves Bidirectional and ADAS Calibration Access Across Nissan’s CONSULT 4 Line - Body Shop Business
passages: Autel U.S. has announced the release of diagnostic and ADAS software updates that expand bidirectional control and ADAS calibration access across Nissan’s supported North American CONSULT 4 vehicle line.
Supporting protected functions on these vehicles required Autel to develop and validate a reliable authorization process compatible with their newer electronic architectures.
The expanded Infiniti QX80 coverage also gives shops access to supported ADAS calibration and wheel-alignment functions on 2024-2025 models.
“This expanded access gives Autel users the ability to perform supported diagnostic and calibration functions through the established AutoAuth authorization process.”
Senior Executive Stew Peregrine, “This is an important step forward for independent shops servicing late-model Nissan vehicles.
Autel has offered AutoAuth-based Nissan security-gateway access for several years on applicable vehicles supported by Nissan’s CONSULT-III plus diagnostic platform.

Access requires an active Autel software subscription, an active AutoAuth account for Nissan access and applicable Autel ADAS calibration software, equipment, targets and accessories when performing a calibration
Nissan began incorporating security-gateway protections into select North American vehicles with the 2020 model year.
These protections restrict access to designated bidirectional functions unless the technician, shop and diagnostic tool are properly authenticated.
Autel demonstrated the breadth of this new capability on a 2026 Nissan Rogue, performing bidirectional diagnostic functions and completing an ADAS calibration live at Auto Glass Week.

Built on the MA600 platform, the MA800 combines dual-laser positioning, mirror alignment and independent pitch, roll and yaw adjustment to help technicians position calibration targets efficiently and accurately.
Eligible users can obtain the software releases through the standard update process on their Autel tablet.
The Nissan diagnostic software is available on supported MaxiSYS Ultra and Ultra S2 tablets.
Jason Stahl talks with Consolidation Coach Director of M&A Chad Smith on private equity’s emerging interest in ADAS calibration businesses.
Microlearning on ADAS calibration, EV powertrains and standards will offer repair shops actionable steps to speed R&D, ensure safe mods and stay compliant.

Supported Autel tablets access protected vehicle functions through AutoAuth, an independently operated service that works with automotive manufacturers and aftermarket tool providers to verify shops, technicians and tools for secure vehicle access.
Available functions vary by vehicle, model year, trim, system and software configuration.
Technicians should confirm coverage for the specific vehicle and procedure through their Autel diagnostic tablet before beginning service.

extraction.body: Apple Watch Series 12 has been a marvel of an upgrade, at least for me. I’ve written about it many times , and personally – I have found that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a competent replacement for the WHOOP . That said, in my past month testing it, there’s one WHOOP feature I’ve found myself missing. Yes, I know – the Series 12 is old news, and there are much cooler things to think about, like iPhone Duo and HomeView . That said, the Apple Watch Series 12 was quite charming to me, primarily because it felt like a little bit of a surprise. We knew we’d be getting an always-on heart rate monitor, and we knew Apple was working on a new Health app, though we didn’t know when it would ship. Seeing the two together actually felt like quite a novel launch. That’s besides the point, though. Let’s talk about the redesigned Health app and what I feel it’s missing. Frankly, Apple did a lot really well here. For one, there’s the fact that the interface actually feels easy to read and navigate. On top of that, the new features like Readiness and Health Age make it feel like a much more meaningful app. Plus, existing features like Vitals and Sleep being integrated means I’ll actually go look at it daily. This Health app isn’t shipping yet. It was available in iOS 27.2 for a little while, but has since been removed . Apple says it’ll come back in a later iOS beta prior to releasing it later this year. In all likelihood, this means iOS 27.3, which should enter beta before the end of the month and ship before the end of December. For me, and this is more of a small personal preference than a true flaw with the app or how it’s designed, I’d really like to see Apple copy WHOOP’s approach to measuring days: sleep. With WHOOP , your days aren’t measured on a fixed 24 hour clock, they’re based on when you go to sleep. That means if you do a workout past midnight, it still counts for the existing day. Or, if you were out late at night, your walk home counts towards the day that you started on, rather than counting towards the next day. I personally prefer this concept of tracking fitness goals. Of course, it could be an option, though I do think fixing peoples “days” to their sleep is a little more sensible than basing it on a normal clock, especially when it comes to tracking exercise. extraction.body: Typically, software updates introduce new features rather than taking them away. So, when you install watchOS 27 on your compatible Apple Watch, you probably aren't surprised to see updates like Siri AI or a step counter on the watch face. But you might be taken aback by what's missing—a multitasking feature that your Apple Watch has had for years. As a result, users running the beta over the summer, or those who updated in September, were likely confused when double-clicking the Digital Crown: On watchOS 26 and earlier, that gesture pulls up a menu with all open apps, similar to the app switcher on iPhone. This allows you to quickly return to a previously used app without needing to dive into the "honeycomb" main app menu.With watchOS 27, that's no longer the case. In their place, Apple is pushing its new "Dynamic app grid." When you press the Digital Crown once, you'll see this new menu, which features the apps Siri thinks you're most likely to use. That might include recently used apps, but also apps you frequently use, even if you haven't used them in a while. The honeycomb menu can certainly make apps difficult to find, especially if you have a lot of them on your watch. But replacing the app switcher entirely doesn't make much sense: There's no guarantee Siri is going to list the recently used app you want to use on the new menu, so you might be forced to manually hunt for it anyway, whereas with the app switcher, you could quickly bounce back to any app, provided you had opened it recently. This isn't the only feature Apple removed with watchOS 27—the company also discontinued the Walkie-Talkie feature with the update. But it looks like it won't be gone for long.The watchOS app switcher is coming backIt seems Apple is changing its mind (or coming to its senses): 9to5Mac recently spotted that the app switcher is back as of the watchOS 27.2 beta. Apple didn't make a note of the addition in any changelogs, so it's unclear why the company undid the change, but it's a welcome recursion—though at this point, there's no guarantee it will make it to the official build of watchOS 27.2. If you're hoping for similar news about Walkie-Talkie, unfortunately that feature has officially been discontinued, so don't expect to see it in a future update. Speaking of which, the only way to try watchOS 27.2 now is to install the watchOS beta on your Apple Watch. That's a risky venture, since you can't downgrade back to watchOS 27 if something goes wrong.

extraction.body: Apple Watch Series 12 has been a marvel of an upgrade, at least for me. I’ve written about it many times , and personally – I have found that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a competent replacement for the WHOOP . That said, in my past month testing it, there’s one WHOOP feature I’ve found myself missing. Yes, I know – the Series 12 is old news, and there are much cooler things to think about, like iPhone Duo and HomeView . That said, the Apple Watch Series 12 was quite charming to me, primarily because it felt like a little bit of a surprise. We knew we’d be getting an always-on heart rate monitor, and we knew Apple was working on a new Health app, though we didn’t know when it would ship. Seeing the two together actually felt like quite a novel launch. That’s besides the point, though. Let’s talk about the redesigned Health app and what I feel it’s missing. Frankly, Apple did a lot really well here. For one, there’s the fact that the interface actually feels easy to read and navigate. On top of that, the new features like Readiness and Health Age make it feel like a much more meaningful app. Plus, existing features like Vitals and Sleep being integrated means I’ll actually go look at it daily. This Health app isn’t shipping yet. It was available in iOS 27.2 for a little while, but has since been removed . Apple says it’ll come back in a later iOS beta prior to releasing it later this year. In all likelihood, this means iOS 27.3, which should enter beta before the end of the month and ship before the end of December. For me, and this is more of a small personal preference than a true flaw with the app or how it’s designed, I’d really like to see Apple copy WHOOP’s approach to measuring days: sleep. With WHOOP , your days aren’t measured on a fixed 24 hour clock, they’re based on when you go to sleep. That means if you do a workout past midnight, it still counts for the existing day. Of course, it could be an option, though I do think fixing peoples “days” to their sleep is a little more sensible than basing it on a normal clock, especially when it comes to tracking exercise. extraction.body: “ I think most people don’t think about this.” That’s what Computer Science Professor Susan Landau told me about surveillance and cybersecurity. Landau, a founding member of the Tufts Cybersecurity Center for the Public Good, is an expert in cybersecurity and privacy and is keenly aware of how we are tracked and monitored in day-to-day life. I spoke to Landau in light of the public reckoning surrounding surveillance and, more specifically, criticism of Flock Safety. Flock, a company known primarily for its license plate-reading technology, has come under fire for oversurveillance of U.S. cities. Groups like DeFlock, a n open-source mapping project, have made it their mission to identify and share the location of Flock cameras around the country. A Flock spokesperson said no team members were available for an interview with the Daily. Privacy has also been a long-held concern for Tufts students. Tufts’ Video Security Policy was drafted between 2012 and 2014 and finalized in 2014. The policy, as presented on the Department of Public Safety’s website, has not been updated since then. In 2017, the Daily published an investigative series about security cameras on campus; several students criticized the video security policy and practices, finding them either invasive or unnecessary. All of this raises the question: Are any of us really aware of how we’re being monitored? To get a better sense of how surveillance and data collection impact Tufts students, I asked Yolanda Smith, chief of police and associate vice president of the Department of Public Safety, and Lorna Koppel, chief information security officer, for statements . Data is collected every time a Tufts student taps or swipes their ID card on campus. “ID card tap records collect basic transaction data required for physical access control, including the name/location of the badge reader, date and time, badge number, and associated individual’s name,” Koppel wrote . However, Koppel clarified that this information isn’t continuously tracked or monitored — it is only reviewed upon request or in light of a security concern. “The system does not analyze, track, or process this data to map individual routines, frequency of visits, or movement patterns across campus. These logs are stored on secured servers within Tufts data centers, with access strictly limited to designated staff based on role-based access permissions, in case access to them is requested due to a legally required or permissible inquiry pursuant to law or university policy or procedure such as an investigation or litigation,” Koppel wrote. Using Tufts’ Wi-Fi network also collects user data. However, this data is encrypted, so most of the time Tufts Technology Services cannot, or does not, see what users are doing on particular sites. “Network and WiFi logging captures standard network metadata required to route traffic and maintain network stability. Most web traffic is encrypted, meaning TTS cannot view or access the actual content of user activity,” Koppel wrote. Video security is also a key element of student privacy discussions. If you walk around campus, you’ll see security cameras in and outside of almost every single building. While preparing to write this article, I made an effort to look out for security cameras as I entered and exited buildings. Every time I made myself aware of the possibility that I was being recorded, I spotted a security camera. “Students should expect cameras in many shared and public areas, such as building entrances, parking areas, and other typical locations,” Smith wrote. “Being recorded is different from being watched: under normal conditions, no one views the footage, and it is reviewed only for a legitimate safety purpose, such as a reported incident or an alarm.” Smith noted that the number of cameras on campus, as well as their specific locations, are not publicly disclosed. The installation of new cameras is also not publicized. I was not surprised to see a high level of video security on campus . I was curious, though, about the storage and use of that footage. Smith noted that, barring particular exceptions, university policy states that footage is to be erased after 30 days. “Recordings are stored in a secure university location for no more than 30 days and are then erased or overwritten. Exceptions include footage retained for a criminal investigation, a court proceeding, or another use approved by the AVP or designee, and certain higher-security areas where retention may be longer. Only designated personnel can play back footage, and all downloads are logged,” Smith wrote. Student information is indeed collected through meal swipes, network use and security camera footage, but is only reviewed or investigated following an alarm or report. In 2024, one Tufts student said that a combination of these types of information led to probation following their involvement in pro-Palestine protests. Smith said that, under university policy, peaceful protest does not justify footage review. However, a perceived or real ‘security risk’ does provoke footage or tap access review. “Video security cameras aren’t used as the principal investigative tool for non-violent and non-destructive minor offenses. It doesn’t prevent reviewing footage after an incident is reported, and the policy separately allows monitoring of special events for safety. The policy also bars monitoring based on protected characteristics and requires that monitoring be based on behavior. A peaceful protest is not a crime, and we do not use cameras to identify people for taking part in a peaceful protest. When there is a security risk or a potential that a crime has occurred, such as vandalism to university property or an assault, there is a public safety reason to review the cameras,” Smith wrote. Smith also noted that Tufts does not employ facial recognition technology. “Tufts does not use facial recognition on its camera system for students or anyone else. The policy’s reference to “digital analytics” means (e.g., motion-based alerts), not identifying individuals,” Smith wrote. Koppel and Smith made clear that university policy does prohibit the viewing of data or footage without a designated need. “University policy strictly prohibits viewing or accessing non-public institutional data without a clear, job-required need,” Koppel wrote. I asked Smith who gets to determine what constitutes ‘need’ in these circumstances. “TUPD operates the system, stores the footage, and decides on law enforcement and investigative use. The AVP or a designee approves those requests, including requests from outside police agencies; all other requests are reviewed in consultation with other university administrators including the General Counsel,” Smith wrote. By using university systems and networks, students are agreeing or opting in to certain levels of data collection. Landau mentioned the importance of the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, though, and noted that Tufts faculty and staff must and do comply with students’ right to privacy. “ Faculty have to be careful, and the university has to be careful, in collection and storage of student data,” Landau said. Although students might only have a vague sense of how their information is collected and stored, Landau told me that her conversations with TTS have not been troubling. “ The last time I talked to our chief security officer, I found that the way Tufts was considering security was thoughtful,” Landau said. “It may not be what students expect, but it definitely was thoughtful.”

Tufts is among few Boston-area colleges and universities who have directly announced official protocols addressing ICE and Department of Homeland Security presence on campus. Some students at other Boston-area schools said in interviews with The Daily Free Press that they wish their schools had more transparency about their ICE policies.

Lokesh, the chair of Northeastern University’s Young Democratic Socialists of America who asked to be identified by their first name due to privacy concerns, said there was “no information whatsoever regarding any ICE policy at Northeastern.”

Northeastern’s YDSA, along with chapters at colleges across Boston, have advocated for sanctuary campus policies, which often prevent college police departments from collaborating with ICE and require ICE to have valid, signed judicial warrants to enter campus.
Northeastern’s YDSA held a “ Town Hall ” meeting in Oct. 2025, where the main concern students raised was the lack of information about the university’s ICE policies, Lokesh said.
“What this creates is fear,” they said. “People are scared because they don’t know what will or will not happen if ICE shows up at their front door.”
Northeastern University declined The Daily Free Press’ request for comment.

An anti-racist student organization at Boston College, FACES , called on their school to issue a statement about ICE after a marked ICE vehicle was allegedly spotted at Ignatius Church — a parish frequented by Boston College students — in Sept. 2025.

“Boston College claims to reject ‘all forms of harassment, wrongful discrimination, and disrespect,’ yet there has been a complete lack of communication on the part of BC’s administration addressing this sensitive issue,” according to the statement from FACES.
Boston College has not put out a formal statement about the incident or about any ICE activity in Boston or around campus.

Anika Obrecht, a senior at Boston College and a senator for the Undergraduate Student Government of Boston College, said the school’s policy in case of ICE activity near campus is to contact the Boston College Police Department, but that no specific protocols have been given out by the University.

“BC has not directly addressed [ICE activity] as an issue. I think they’re trying to keep it very internally managed,” said Obrecht. “On the international student side of things, I think it’s really scary for them, and there isn’t a lot of conversation or protocol in place to guide them.”
Boston College did not respond to The Daily Free Press’ request for comment.
According to BU spokesperson Colin Riley, BU has not received any reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement on campus.
However, ICE activity has been reported in communities around campus, such as Allston, including a raid on Allston Car Wash, which is about one mile off campus.

The co-chair of Back Bay YDSA, who requested to go by the pseudonym ‘C’ due to concerns about retribution by BU, said BU ICE Watch, an ICE “hotline” run by BBYDSA, has received multiple calls about ICE activity in Allston and neighboring communities.
C said the main concerns she has heard from students regarding ICE activity is uncertainty about BU’s policies and plan of action in the case of sightings or activity on campus.

“The BU websites, as they exist right now, are very unclear about what BU will do if they see ICE on campus,” C said. “They’re not even clear about what kind of warrants, what conditions under which BU would not interfere with an ICE presence on campus.”
BU’s website states BUPD will work with university officials to respond “in accordance with the law” if immigration authorities seek to arrest or detain students or request information.

BBYDSA has advocated for sanctuary campus policies, such as requiring a judicial warrant for ICE to be allowed on campus and notifying students or staff members if their information is requested by ICE.

“But it’s been a year [and] the school hasn’t met a single demand,” C said. “And also, it’s becoming very clear that ICE doesn’t care about due process anyway. So any sort of reform that we win from the school … would not be enough to protect immigrant workers and students at BU.”

Landau, a founding member of the Tufts Cybersecurity Center for the Public Good, is an expert in cybersecurity and privacy and is keenly aware of how we are tracked and monitored in day-to-day life. I spoke to Landau in light of the public reckoning surrounding surveillance and, more specifically, criticism of Flock Safety. Flock, a company known primarily for its license plate-reading technology, has come under fire for oversurveillance of U.S. cities. Groups like DeFlock, a n open-source mapping project, have made it their mission to identify and share the location of Flock cameras around the country. A Flock spokesperson said no team members were available for an interview with the Daily. Privacy has also been a long-held concern for Tufts students. Tufts’ Video Security Policy was drafted between 2012 and 2014 and finalized in 2014. The policy, as presented on the Department of Public Safety’s website, has not been updated since then. In 2017, the Daily published an investigative series about security cameras on campus; several students criticized the video security policy and practices, finding them either invasive or unnecessary. All of this raises the question: Are any of us really aware of how we’re being monitored? To get a better sense of how surveillance and data collection impact Tufts students, I asked Yolanda Smith, chief of police and associate vice president of the Department of Public Safety, and Lorna Koppel, chief information security officer, for statements . Data is collected every time a Tufts student taps or swipes their ID card on campus. “ID card tap records collect basic transaction data required for physical access control, including the name/location of the badge reader, date and time, badge number, and associated individual’s name,” Koppel wrote . However, Koppel clarified that this information isn’t continuously tracked or monitored — it is only reviewed upon request or in light of a security concern. “The system does not analyze, track, or process this data to map individual routines, frequency of visits, or movement patterns across campus. These logs are stored on secured servers within Tufts data centers, with access strictly limited to designated staff based on role-based access permissions, in case access to them is requested due to a legally required or permissible inquiry pursuant to law or university policy or procedure such as an investigation or litigation,” Koppel wrote. Using Tufts’ Wi-Fi network also collects user data. However, this data is encrypted, so most of the time Tufts Technology Services cannot, or does not, see what users are doing on particular sites. “Network and WiFi logging captures standard network metadata required to route traffic and maintain network stability. Most web traffic is encrypted, meaning TTS cannot view or access the actual content of user activity,” Koppel wrote. Video security is also a key element of student privacy discussions. If you walk around campus, you’ll see security cameras in and outside of almost every single building. While preparing to write this article, I made an effort to look out for security cameras as I entered and exited buildings. Every time I made myself aware of the possibility that I was being recorded, I spotted a security camera. “Students should expect cameras in many shared and public areas, such as building entrances, parking areas, and other typical locations,” Smith wrote. “Being recorded is different from being watched: under normal conditions, no one views the footage, and it is reviewed only for a legitimate safety purpose, such as a reported incident or an alarm.” Smith noted that the number of cameras on campus, as well as their specific locations, are not publicly disclosed. The installation of new cameras is also not publicized. I was not surprised to see a high level of video security on campus . I was curious, though, about the storage and use of that footage. Smith noted that, barring particular exceptions, university policy states that footage is to be erased after 30 days. “Recordings are stored in a secure university location for no more than 30 days and are then erased or overwritten. Exceptions include footage retained for a criminal investigation, a court proceeding, or another use approved by the AVP or designee, and certain higher-security areas where retention may be longer. Only designated personnel can play back footage, and all downloads are logged,” Smith wrote. Student information is indeed collected through meal swipes, network use and security camera footage, but is only reviewed or investigated following an alarm or report. In 2024, one Tufts student said that a combination of these types of information led to probation following their involvement in pro-Palestine protests. Smith said that, under university policy, peaceful protest does not justify footage review. However, a perceived or real ‘security risk’ does provoke footage or tap access review. “Video security cameras aren’t used as the principal investigative tool for non-violent and non-destructive minor offenses. It doesn’t prevent reviewing footage after an incident is reported, and the policy separately allows monitoring of special events for safety. The policy also bars monitoring based on protected characteristics and requires that monitoring be based on behavior. A peaceful protest is not a crime, and we do not use cameras to identify people for taking part in a peaceful protest. When there is a security risk or a potential that a crime has occurred, such as vandalism to university property or an assault, there is a public safety reason to review the cameras,” Smith wrote. Smith also noted that Tufts does not employ facial recognition technology. “Tufts does not use facial recognition on its camera system for students or anyone else. The policy’s reference to “digital analytics” means (e.g., motion-based alerts), not identifying individuals,” Smith wrote. Koppel and Smith made clear that university policy does prohibit the viewing of data or footage without a designated need. “University policy strictly prohibits viewing or accessing non-public institutional data without a clear, job-required need,” Koppel wrote. I asked Smith who gets to determine what constitutes ‘need’ in these circumstances. “TUPD operates the system, stores the footage, and decides on law enforcement and investigative use. The AVP or a designee approves those requests, including requests from outside police agencies; all other requests are reviewed in consultation with other university administrators including the General Counsel,” Smith wrote. By using university systems and networks, students are agreeing or opting in to certain levels of data collection. Landau mentioned the importance of the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, though, and noted that Tufts faculty and staff must and do comply with students’ right to privacy. “ Faculty have to be careful, and the university has to be careful, in collection and storage of student data,” Landau said. Although students might only have a vague sense of how their information is collected and stored, Landau told me that her conversations with TTS have not been troubling. “ The last time I talked to our chief security officer, I found that the way Tufts was considering security was thoughtful,” Landau said. “It may not be what students expect, but it definitely was thoughtful.”

passages: Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy are developing methods to detect hardware tampering and build chips resistant to both physical manipulation and future quantum attacks.
The team uses open-source software, HAL, to analyze chip schematics and is proactively enhancing open-source chips with quantum-secure circuits.
“Manipulation deep within a chip would be almost impossible to detect – and could threaten entire infrastructures.”
The institute’s concerns extend beyond detecting existing tampering to proactively fortifying future chip designs.

“Quantum computers pose a threat to end-to-end encryption in messaging services and security measures used in online financial transactions, for example,” demonstrating the urgency of this preventative approach.

Reconstructing a chip’s netlist, the detailed map of its internal connections, is proving essential for uncovering subtle hardware tampering, a process that can introduce vulnerabilities undetectable through software-based security measures.

“We are simply adding a few new instructions to an existing chip,” Pham explains, outlining a method that allows circuits to support both conventional and quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms during the transition to a post-quantum world.
The institute suggests that relying on post-quantum cryptography now, and ideally using open-source technology is the most prudent course of action.

The team’s work builds on the understanding that software updates are insufficient to address deeply embedded hardware manipulation, as “Software can be updated,” but physical alterations remain persistent and difficult to detect.

“Most HAL users are companies working in security-related fields,” explains Julian Speith, a postdoctoral researcher involved in the software’s development, indicating a practical demand for tools that can proactively assess chip trustworthiness.

“In theory, a manufacturer like Huawei in China could build a ‘kill switch’ into its chips and then use a secret command to shut down all cell towers with Huawei hardware in Germany,” a stark illustration of the geopolitical implications of compromised hardware.

While HAL currently focuses on identifying these hidden functions within reconstructed netlists, the ultimate goal is to build security directly into the chip’s design, making tampering significantly more difficult and detectable.

This capability is particularly vital in detecting hardware Trojans, circuits intentionally embedded to create security vulnerabilities and compromise data integrity, a standard scenario in related research.
Manufacturers rarely provide detailed documentation outlining chip functions, further complicating the analysis process and highlighting the need for reverse engineering tools like HAL.

While physically opening these chips is established practice, determining the function of identical-looking transistors remains a significant hurdle, as manufacturer-specific hardware lacks accompanying documentation detailing operational areas.

extraction.body: Software can be updated. Hardware cannot. Manipulation deep within a chip would be almost impossible to detect—and could threaten entire infrastructures. At the same time, it is now more important than ever that we prepare hardware for impending attacks using quantum computers. They are everywhere, but largely invisible: integrated circuits, better known as chips, can be found in pretty much every technical device nowadays. They wake us up in the morning, help us navigate through traffic, connect us with friends and colleagues. Without these small black blocks with their little silver legs, there is very little in modern societies that would function. No internet. No smartphones. No transportation. In most cases, not even refrigerators or washing machines. The security of this omnipresent hardware is therefore of increasing importance in our digital society. Whereas software bugs or risks caused by malware can often be fixed with updates, manipulation at the hardware level is more critical: hardware is embedded deep in the system, and errors are much harder to detect. If a chip's hardwired circuits are manipulated, this can alter its behavior in ways that are invisible: commands are tampered with, security mechanisms bypassed, and trust becomes an illusion. While the proverbial "smoking gun"—that is, irrefutable proof of deliberately built-in, secret backdoors in chips—is still missing, there are often indications that state-level players are interfering with hardware systems. For example, as early as the late 1980s, the Swiss company Crypto AG came under suspicion of having sold intentionally weakened encryption technology in collaboration with the CIA in the U.S. and BND in Germany. "Operation Rubicon," which later came to light, confirmed that both intelligence agencies had controlled the company for decades. The information revealed by Edward Snowden also provided evidence of hardware implants. According to reports, as part of the NSA's "Interdiction" method, electronic devices were secretly intercepted during transport, opened, and fitted with surveillance or tampering components before being delivered. The current geopolitical upheavals, and Europe's much-discussed digital sovereignty, are bringing hardware security increasingly into focus. Although Europe is strong when it comes to designing chips, it has virtually no manufacturing capacity of its own, and is thus reliant on other countries for chip production. "Pretty much all circuits that surround us, as well as our entire digital wireless infrastructure, rely on chips made in Taiwan, China, South Korea or, to a small extent, the U.S.," says Christof Paar, who heads the Embedded Security group at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy in Bochum. This requires trust that these manufacturers will implement designs exactly as planned, and will not, for example, build hidden backdoors into the chips under government pressure. Such manipulations could enable remote control of the hardware by third parties. "In theory, a manufacturer like Huawei in China could build a 'kill switch' into its chips and then use a secret command to shut down all cell towers with Huawei hardware in Germany," says Paar. He is therefore working to identify security vulnerabilities in computer hardware together with his colleagues while, at the same time, finding ways to make hardware production more trustworthy—before anything happens. One obvious, yet important, method for achieving this is the rigorous testing of new chips. "For example, when a certification body receives a cellular base station or a smartphone chip, it can investigate whether the chip can be put into a state, using a specific input, in which it suddenly reacts differently from how it is supposed to," explains Paar. Such anomalies could be an initial indication of tampering. However, in order to truly understand how an unknown chip works down to the last detail, a much more drastic measure is required: forcibly opening it to take a look at its innermost parts. This is an extremely complex, multistep process that demands the highest precision, and often pushes the limits of what is financially and technically feasible. "It's like having to create a map by carefully stitching together many small photos," explains Paar. And in practice, of course, this process is never perfect. A complete, physical analysis of a modern microprocessor with billions of transistors, like a computer's CPU, is unrealistic in any case. The cost and time required would be astronomical. For smaller chips, such as those found in bank cards, physically opening and analyzing them has been standard practice for many years now. But even in these supposedly "easy" cases, there are problems. For example, the transistors in images of an opened chip all look exactly the same. Even if it is possible to see where the connections between them run, it is very difficult to determine the functions they perform from that alone. After all, manufacturer-specific hardware does not come with a user handbook that would reveal which area of the chip performs which function. While the netlist contains information on the individual transistors and their connections, it still lacks any labels or explanations as to which functions they perform. In order to determine how a complete chip works using the netlist, Paar and his colleagues developed their own open-source software: HAL. HAL is more than just a reference to the powerful computer HAL 9000 from the science fiction classic "2001: A Space Odyssey"; it also stands for Hardware Analyzer. The software analyzes netlists, and thus helps to determine whether a chip really does only what it promises, and whether it acts against the user's interests by, for example, secretly sending data to the outside world. "Most HAL users are companies working in security-related fields," says Julian Speith, who was involved in developing the software as a postdoc in Paar's group. "We have had inquiries from government research laboratories and agencies, for example." An important use case for HAL is the detection of hardware Trojans. These are circuits integrated intentionally into electronic components that enable unauthorized access to, for example, spy on a user's confidential data. So far, HAL has not detected any such manipulation. Such changes would be extremely difficult to find, however, as there is no typical pattern to search for. To test their software, HAL's developers therefore designed a virtual chip, and intentionally added an additional signal wire that HAL was supposed to help users identify. Under certain conditions, this hidden component transmits a secret cryptographic key via the chip's output. "If attackers know how to activate this function, they can simply read the key via the output," explains Speith. "This is a standard scenario in the research on hardware Trojans." However, HAL has not been designed to be a fully automatic vulnerability scanner, because there are simply too many possible Trojans of this kind to take account of. Its strength lies in showing analysts the relevant areas in a chip. The actual security assessment—i.e., determining whether an irregularity is in fact an unintentional vulnerability or a deliberately embedded Trojan—is left to the humans. "Ultimately, HAL is also there to make this subject more accessible to the general public, because up until now, the vast majority of it has been hidden behind closed doors," says Speith. Malicious actors who secretly modify chips are not the only threat to the security of modern hardware. Many algorithms that are hardwired into chips via a specific sequence of logic gates and other components and that perform encryption functions there could be cracked quickly by the quantum computers of the future. "Quantum computers pose a threat to end-to-end encryption in messaging services and security measures used in online financial transactions, for example," says Hoang Nguyen Hien Pham. As a doctoral researcher in the Cryptographic Engineering Group of Peter Schwabe at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy, she is working on making algorithms embedded in cryptographic chips "future-proof." In this regard, experts like Pham speak of a "migration" from classical cryptography to post-quantum cryptography. The encryption algorithms this requires should be able to stump even quantum computers in the future, and they have now been devised and standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist). However, to ensure they run efficiently on devices such as laptops, smartphones, or even on credit cards, their hardware must also be adapted. Institutions like NIST, but also the EU, have set deadlines for this by around 2030, and major companies such as Google, Amazon, and Microsoft want to complete their migrations within a similar time frame. Then, when the news finally breaks that quantum computers are actually ready to crack real-world systems, it shouldn't be too much of a shock for the world. "It will be a long-awaited milestone, and we are already very well prepared for it," says Pham, reassuringly. "Many apps, such as WhatsApp or Signal, have already started the migration process." Essentially, the new "quantum-secure" algorithms could also run on existing security-related hardware systems—albeit very slowly and inefficiently. Developing completely new chips for this purpose, on the other hand, would be overkill, as it would demand an enormous amount of effort and expense. The goal of Pham and her colleagues is therefore to adapt current security chips to future requirements with as few changes as possible. "We are simply adding a few new instructions to an existing chip," says the researcher. This should also ensure that circuits support both classical and quantum-secure cryptographic algorithms at the same time during the transition period. Pham and her colleagues based their work on the OpenTitan security chip, which serves as the foundation for the security of the entire device on laptops such as the Chromebook. It checks whether the installed software has been tampered with as soon as the device is turned on, manages cryptographic keys, and ensures that a device can authenticate itself as genuine to other systems. Pham advises users to start by developing a basic awareness of the security of the apps they use on a daily basis. In addition, she recommends, wherever possible, using apps that are already prepared for the quantum age. Even if quantum computers are still a few years away, attackers could already be intercepting encrypted information under the motto "harvest now, decrypt later," and storing it until new technology is finally available for decryption. "It's better to rely on post-quantum cryptography now, and ideally on open-source technology," urges the researcher. After all, openness is widely regarded as the key to secure hardware. And only when the technology is publicly available will specialists around the world be able to examine it, in order to understand exactly how it works—and quickly report any security vulnerabilities. This applies not only to the post-quantum world, but also to the dangers posed by maliciously manipulated hardware: the more open a design is, the harder it is to build a secret "backdoor." Or, as cryptographer Paar puts it: "Transparency creates trust." BSc Life Sciences & Ecology. Microbiology lab background with pharmaceutical news experience in oil, gas, and renewable industries.
