These are circuits integrated intentionally into electronic components that enable unauthorized access to, for example, spy on a user's confidential data. So far, HAL has not detected any such manipulation. Such changes would be extremely difficult to find, however, as there is no typical pattern to search for.

To test their software, HAL's developers therefore designed a virtual chip, and intentionally added an additional signal wire that HAL was supposed to help users identify. Under certain conditions, this hidden component transmits a secret cryptographic key via the chip's output. "If attackers know how to activate this function, they can simply read the key via the output," explains Speith. "This is a standard scenario in the research on hardware Trojans."

However, HAL has not been designed to be a fully automatic vulnerability scanner, because there are simply too many possible Trojans of this kind to take account of. Its strength lies in showing analysts the relevant areas in a chip. The actual security assessment—i.e., determining whether an irregularity is in fact an unintentional vulnerability or a deliberately embedded Trojan—is left to the humans.
"Ultimately, HAL is also there to make this subject more accessible to the general public, because up until now, the vast majority of it has been hidden behind closed doors," says Speith.

Malicious actors who secretly modify chips are not the only threat to the security of modern hardware. Many algorithms that are hardwired into chips via a specific sequence of logic gates and other components and that perform encryption functions there could be cracked quickly by the quantum computers of the future.

"Quantum computers pose a threat to end-to-end encryption in messaging services and security measures used in online financial transactions, for example," says Hoang Nguyen Hien Pham. As a doctoral researcher in the Cryptographic Engineering Group of Peter Schwabe at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy, she is working on making algorithms embedded in cryptographic chips "future-proof."

In this regard, experts like Pham speak of a "migration" from classical cryptography to post-quantum cryptography. The encryption algorithms this requires should be able to stump even quantum computers in the future, and they have now been devised and standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist). However, to ensure they run efficiently on devices such as laptops, smartphones, or even on credit cards, their hardware must also be adapted.

Institutions like NIST, but also the EU, have set deadlines for this by around 2030, and major companies such as Google, Amazon, and Microsoft want to complete their migrations within a similar time frame. Then, when the news finally breaks that quantum computers are actually ready to crack real-world systems, it shouldn't be too much of a shock for the world.
"It will be a long-awaited milestone, and we are already very well prepared for it," says Pham, reassuringly. "Many apps, such as WhatsApp or Signal, have already started the migration process."

Essentially, the new "quantum-secure" algorithms could also run on existing security-related hardware systems—albeit very slowly and inefficiently. Developing completely new chips for this purpose, on the other hand, would be overkill, as it would demand an enormous amount of effort and expense.

The goal of Pham and her colleagues is therefore to adapt current security chips to future requirements with as few changes as possible. "We are simply adding a few new instructions to an existing chip," says the researcher. This should also ensure that circuits support both classical and quantum-secure cryptographic algorithms at the same time during the transition period.

Pham and her colleagues based their work on the OpenTitan security chip, which serves as the foundation for the security of the entire device on laptops such as the Chromebook. It checks whether the installed software has been tampered with as soon as the device is turned on, manages cryptographic keys, and ensures that a device can authenticate itself as genuine to other systems.

Pham advises users to start by developing a basic awareness of the security of the apps they use on a daily basis. In addition, she recommends, wherever possible, using apps that are already prepared for the quantum age.

Even if quantum computers are still a few years away, attackers could already be intercepting encrypted information under the motto "harvest now, decrypt later," and storing it until new technology is finally available for decryption. "It's better to rely on post-quantum cryptography now, and ideally on open-source technology," urges the researcher.

After all, openness is widely regarded as the key to secure hardware. And only when the technology is publicly available will specialists around the world be able to examine it, in order to understand exactly how it works—and quickly report any security vulnerabilities.

This applies not only to the post-quantum world, but also to the dangers posed by maliciously manipulated hardware: the more open a design is, the harder it is to build a secret "backdoor." Or, as cryptographer Paar puts it: "Transparency creates trust."

The team uses open-source software, HAL, to analyze chip schematics and is proactively enhancing open-source chips with quantum-secure circuits. “Manipulation deep within a chip would be almost impossible to detect – and could threaten entire infrastructures.” This capability is particularly vital in detecting hardware Trojans, circuits intentionally embedded to create security vulnerabilities and compromise data integrity, a standard scenario in related research. While HAL does not function as a fully automated vulnerability scanner due to the sheer variety of potential Trojan designs, it effectively narrows the search for analysts, highlighting areas of interest within a complex chip layout. The software’s utility extends beyond academic research, attracting interest from government research laboratories and agencies, as well as companies focused on security-critical applications. “Most HAL users are companies working in security-related fields,” explains Julian Speith, a postdoctoral researcher involved in the software’s development, indicating a practical demand for tools that can proactively assess chip trustworthiness. This level of scrutiny is becoming increasingly important given the concentration of chip manufacturing in a limited number of global locations. Pretty much all circuits that surround us, as well as our entire digital wireless infrastructure, rely on chips made in Taiwan, China, South Korea or, to a small extent, the USA. Beyond Trojan detection, the institute is also proactively fortifying chip designs against future threats, specifically those posed by quantum computers. Researchers are enhancing open-source chips with quantum-secure circuits, employing encryption methods designed to withstand attacks from these powerful, yet-to-be-fully-realized machines. Every Pavona chip manufactured on this basis in the future will automatically include these circuits, ensuring post-quantum cryptography runs efficiently. This approach represents a shift towards building security directly into the hardware, rather than relying solely on software updates to address vulnerabilities. The team’s work acknowledges the inherent difficulties in visually inspecting chip designs for tampering, as transistors often appear identical in images, making it challenging to discern their function based solely on physical appearance. Even with detailed connection maps, determining the purpose of specific chip areas remains a complex task without accompanying documentation. HAL provides an analytical layer, assisting experts in interpreting the detailed web of connections and identifying anomalies. For example, when a certification body receives a cellular base station or a smartphone chip, it can investigate whether the chip can be put into a state, using a specific input, in which it suddenly reacts differently from how it is supposed to. Reconstructing a chip’s netlist, the detailed map of its internal connections, is proving essential for uncovering subtle hardware tampering, a process that can introduce vulnerabilities undetectable through software-based security measures. To validate HAL’s capabilities, the institute’s developers intentionally introduced a hidden signal wire into a virtual chip design, a component designed to leak a cryptographic key under specific conditions. “If attackers know how to activate this function, they can simply read the key via the output,” explained Julian Speith, highlighting the potential for covert data exfiltration. The institute’s concerns extend beyond detecting existing tampering to proactively fortifying future chip designs. The team is actively integrating quantum-secure circuits into open-source chips, creating hardware that can resist attacks from increasingly powerful quantum computers. “Quantum computers pose a threat to end-to-end encryption in messaging services and security measures used in online financial transactions, for example,” demonstrating the urgency of this preventative approach. This isn’t merely a theoretical exercise; the team anticipates a critical juncture in quantum computing’s development. “It will be a long-awaited milestone, and we are already very well-prepared for it,” they state, suggesting a proactive stance against a future threat. The potential for malicious actors to exploit hardware vulnerabilities is not limited to theoretical scenarios. The institute points to the possibility of nation-state actors embedding into chips, enabling them to remotely disable critical infrastructure. “In theory, a manufacturer like Huawei in China could build a ‘kill switch’ into its chips and then use a secret command to shut down all cell towers with Huawei hardware in Germany,” a stark illustration of the geopolitical implications of compromised hardware. While HAL currently focuses on identifying these hidden functions within reconstructed netlists, the ultimate goal is to build security directly into the chip’s design, making tampering significantly more difficult and detectable. Quantum computers pose a threat to end-to-end encryption in messaging services and security measures used in online financial transactions, for example. Minimizing both cost and development time, the team’s approach centers on adapting existing chip designs rather than creating entirely new ones. Developing entirely new chips would be an immense undertaking, demanding resources far beyond the scope of most research groups, but Pham and her colleagues are focused on modifying current security chips to meet future demands with minimal changes. “We are simply adding a few new instructions to an existing chip,” Pham explains, outlining a method that allows circuits to support both conventional and quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms during the transition to a post-quantum world. This adaptation relies heavily on OpenTitan, an open-source chip whose internal workings are publicly accessible, enabling thorough review and enhancement by companies and independent experts. The Max Planck Institute team has integrated their quantum-secure circuits into Pavona, a new project built upon the OpenTitan foundation. The institute suggests that relying on post-quantum cryptography now, and ideally using open-source technology is the most prudent course of action. “It’s better to rely on post-quantum cryptography now, and ideally on open-source technology,” they state, advocating for a collaborative and transparent approach to security. The complexity of analyzing chip circuitry is considerable; reconstructing the layers of metal traces connecting transistors is likened to assembling a map from numerous small photographs. This process, while challenging, is essential for understanding how a chip functions and identifying potential vulnerabilities. Pretty much all circuits that surround us, as well as our entire digital wireless infrastructure, rely on chips made in Taiwan, China, South Korea or, to a small extent, the USA. The challenge lies in the sheer number of potential Trojan implementations, preventing fully automated scanning and requiring analysts to focus on areas flagged by HAL. Transistors appear identical in imagery, making functional determination from connections alone a complex task. Manufacturers rarely provide detailed documentation outlining chip functions, further complicating the analysis process and highlighting the need for reverse engineering tools like HAL. This reliance on reconstruction emphasises the vulnerability inherent in complex supply chains, where verifying the integrity of components becomes increasingly difficult as designs are outsourced and manufacturing processes become more opaque. Openness, according to the researchers, is paramount to building trust in hardware security. This approach contrasts with proprietary designs, where security relies on secrecy, a strategy that becomes less effective as reverse engineering tools become more sophisticated. The team is actively applying this principle by developing open-source chips enhanced with quantum-secure circuits, providing a transparent foundation for future hardware security. The integration of these quantum-secure circuits isn’t simply a future-proofing measure. It’s a proactive step toward mitigating the risks posed by increasingly powerful computing capabilities. The team’s work also addresses the potential for malicious manipulation during manufacturing, citing a scenario where a manufacturer could embed a “kill switch” into chips, allowing remote shutdown of critical infrastructure. This highlights the need for robust verification processes throughout the entire supply chain, from design to fabrication. The team’s methodology acknowledges that complete automation of vulnerability detection is unrealistic, but HAL’s ability to narrow the search area significantly reduces the workload for security analysts. By focusing on reconstructed netlists, the software helps analysts understand the chip’s intended behavior and identify deviations that could indicate malicious intent. This combination of automated analysis and human expertise represents a pragmatic approach to addressing the growing threat of hardware tampering and ensuring the integrity of critical systems. In theory, a manufacturer like Huawei in China could build a ‘kill switch’ into its chips and then use a secret command to shut down all cell towers with Huawei hardware in Germany. The reconstruction of a chip’s circuit diagram, known as a netlist, demands painstaking work even for smaller components like those found in bank cards, a process refined over many years of practical application. While physically opening these chips is established practice, determining the function of identical-looking transistors remains a significant hurdle, as manufacturer-specific hardware lacks accompanying documentation detailing operational areas. These chips use “gates”, specific transistor connections that perform logical operations, as fundamental building blocks, allowing researchers to trace signal pathways and understand the chip’s intended behavior. The open-source software HAL analyzes reconstructed chip schematics known as netlists, and identifies possible hardware Trojans, which are additional circuits that create security vulnerabilities. Each layer demands thousands of individual images at high resolution, demonstrating the intricacy of modern microelectronics and the scale of the reconstruction task. However, even a complete netlist is insufficient for understanding a chip’s functionality. It lacks the necessary labels and explanations to identify the purpose of individual circuits. “While the netlist contains information on the individual transistors and their connections, it still lacks any labels or explanations as to which functions they perform,” explains the institute, highlighting the need for further analysis to map circuit elements to specific operations. This approach contrasts sharply with relying solely on detecting anomalies in an entirely opaque design, where even subtle alterations can be difficult to discern. Dust and scratches on the chip’s surface can obscure or misrepresent transistors in the images, requiring careful manual review to ensure accuracy. “Even a tiny speck of dust or a scratch on the surface can cause some of the transistors in an image to be obscured or misinterpreted,” notes the institute, emphasising the challenges of physical analysis. The team’s work builds on the understanding that software updates are insufficient to address deeply embedded hardware manipulation, as “Software can be updated,” but physical alterations remain persistent and difficult to detect. The team’s goal is to provide tools and techniques that allow for more thorough and reliable hardware verification, ultimately enhancing the security of critical infrastructure and protecting against increasingly sophisticated attacks. Anyone who wants to manipulate a chip ultimately has to replace or modify certain gates – and it is precisely this process that has to be made as difficult as possible through clever design. extraction.body: Software can be updated. Hardware cannot. Manipulation deep within a chip would be almost impossible to detect—and could threaten entire infrastructures. At the same time, it is now more important than ever that we prepare hardware for impending attacks using quantum computers. They are everywhere, but largely invisible: integrated circuits, better known as chips, can be found in pretty much every technical device nowadays. They wake us up in the morning, help us navigate through traffic, connect us with friends and colleagues. Without these small black blocks with their little silver legs, there is very little in modern societies that would function. No internet. No smartphones. No transportation. In most cases, not even refrigerators or washing machines. The security of this omnipresent hardware is therefore of increasing importance in our digital society. Whereas software bugs or risks caused by malware can often be fixed with updates, manipulation at the hardware level is more critical: hardware is embedded deep in the system, and errors are much harder to detect. If a chip's hardwired circuits are manipulated, this can alter its behavior in ways that are invisible: commands are tampered with, security mechanisms bypassed, and trust becomes an illusion. While the proverbial "smoking gun"—that is, irrefutable proof of deliberately built-in, secret backdoors in chips—is still missing, there are often indications that state-level players are interfering with hardware systems. For example, as early as the late 1980s, the Swiss company Crypto AG came under suspicion of having sold intentionally weakened encryption technology in collaboration with the CIA in the U.S. and BND in Germany. "Operation Rubicon," which later came to light, confirmed that both intelligence agencies had controlled the company for decades. The information revealed by Edward Snowden also provided evidence of hardware implants. According to reports, as part of the NSA's "Interdiction" method, electronic devices were secretly intercepted during transport, opened, and fitted with surveillance or tampering components before being delivered. The current geopolitical upheavals, and Europe's much-discussed digital sovereignty, are bringing hardware security increasingly into focus. Although Europe is strong when it comes to designing chips, it has virtually no manufacturing capacity of its own, and is thus reliant on other countries for chip production. "Pretty much all circuits that surround us, as well as our entire digital wireless infrastructure, rely on chips made in Taiwan, China, South Korea or, to a small extent, the U.S.," says Christof Paar, who heads the Embedded Security group at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy in Bochum. This requires trust that these manufacturers will implement designs exactly as planned, and will not, for example, build hidden backdoors into the chips under government pressure. Such manipulations could enable remote control of the hardware by third parties. "In theory, a manufacturer like Huawei in China could build a 'kill switch' into its chips and then use a secret command to shut down all cell towers with Huawei hardware in Germany," says Paar. He is therefore working to identify security vulnerabilities in computer hardware together with his colleagues while, at the same time, finding ways to make hardware production more trustworthy—before anything happens. One obvious, yet important, method for achieving this is the rigorous testing of new chips. "For example, when a certification body receives a cellular base station or a smartphone chip, it can investigate whether the chip can be put into a state, using a specific input, in which it suddenly reacts differently from how it is supposed to," explains Paar. Such anomalies could be an initial indication of tampering. However, in order to truly understand how an unknown chip works down to the last detail, a much more drastic measure is required: forcibly opening it to take a look at its innermost parts. This is an extremely complex, multistep process that demands the highest precision, and often pushes the limits of what is financially and technically feasible. "It's like having to create a map by carefully stitching together many small photos," explains Paar. And in practice, of course, this process is never perfect. A complete, physical analysis of a modern microprocessor with billions of transistors, like a computer's CPU, is unrealistic in any case. The cost and time required would be astronomical. For smaller chips, such as those found in bank cards, physically opening and analyzing them has been standard practice for many years now. But even in these supposedly "easy" cases, there are problems. For example, the transistors in images of an opened chip all look exactly the same. Even if it is possible to see where the connections between them run, it is very difficult to determine the functions they perform from that alone. After all, manufacturer-specific hardware does not come with a user handbook that would reveal which area of the chip performs which function. While the netlist contains information on the individual transistors and their connections, it still lacks any labels or explanations as to which functions they perform. In order to determine how a complete chip works using the netlist, Paar and his colleagues developed their own open-source software: HAL. HAL is more than just a reference to the powerful computer HAL 9000 from the science fiction classic "2001: A Space Odyssey"; it also stands for Hardware Analyzer. The software analyzes netlists, and thus helps to determine whether a chip really does only what it promises, and whether it acts against the user's interests by, for example, secretly sending data to the outside world. "Most HAL users are companies working in security-related fields," says Julian Speith, who was involved in developing the software as a postdoc in Paar's group. "We have had inquiries from government research laboratories and agencies, for example." An important use case for HAL is the detection of hardware Trojans. These are circuits integrated intentionally into electronic components that enable unauthorized access to, for example, spy on a user's confidential data. They are everywhere, but largely invisible: integrated circuits, better known as chips, can be found in pretty much every technical device nowadays. They wake us up in the morning, help us navigate through traffic, connect us with friends and colleagues.

Without these small black blocks with their little silver legs, there is very little in modern societies that would function. No internet. No smartphones. No transportation. In most cases, not even refrigerators or washing machines.

The security of this omnipresent hardware is therefore of increasing importance in our digital society. Whereas software bugs or risks caused by malware can often be fixed with updates, manipulation at the hardware level is more critical: hardware is embedded deep in the system, and errors are much harder to detect.
If a chip's hardwired circuits are manipulated, this can alter its behavior in ways that are invisible: commands are tampered with, security mechanisms bypassed, and trust becomes an illusion.

"Operation Rubicon," which later came to light, confirmed that both intelligence agencies had controlled the company for decades.

The information revealed by Edward Snowden also provided evidence of hardware implants. According to reports, as part of the NSA's "Interdiction" method, electronic devices were secretly intercepted during transport, opened, and fitted with surveillance or tampering components before being delivered.

The current geopolitical upheavals, and Europe's much-discussed digital sovereignty, are bringing hardware security increasingly into focus. Although Europe is strong when it comes to designing chips, it has virtually no manufacturing capacity of its own, and is thus reliant on other countries for chip production.

sources.title: This Cybersecurity Agency Is Supposed to Protect U.S. Elections. Officials Fear It’s Been Compromised by Trump. - ProPublica
passages: Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration.

In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA.

The material included raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing activity being monitored in several states.
Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election.

Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S.

A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.”
Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina.
The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure.
The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public.

In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.
State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even without help from CISA.
Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines .
“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA.
“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security.
“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law.
Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust.
And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

extraction.body: A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request. The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.” While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them. Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.” Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.” Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA. A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.” Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust. At its center was a commitment: The sensitive information states and vendors shared with CISA would be kept confidential. “It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law. Under Director Chris Krebs, CISA hosted penetration testing in which its agents would try to hack into a state’s system to locate weaknesses that could then be patched, along with tabletop exercises simulating a series of potential catastrophes around elections. The material included raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing activity being monitored in several states.
Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election.

Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S.

A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.”
Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina.
The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure.
The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public.

In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.
State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even without help from CISA.
Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines .
“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA.
“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security.
“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law.
Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust.
And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

sources.title: This Cybersecurity Agency Is Supposed to Protect U.S. Elections. Officials Fear It’s Been Compromised by Trump. - ProPublica
passages: Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration.

In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA.

The material included raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing activity being monitored in several states.
Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election.

Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S.

A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.”
Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina.
The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure.
The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public.

In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.
State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even without help from CISA.
Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines .
“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA.
“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security.
“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law.
Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust.
And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request. The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines .
“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA.
“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security.
“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law.
Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust.
And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory.
If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models .

As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out.

According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market.

One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate.

Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers.

SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems.

Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic are all developing custom silicon chips. This provides yet another tailwind for increased memory demand and could help SK Hynix diversify across different AI computing architectures. In other words, SK Hynix doesn't need one chip designer to dominate the AI infrastructure era indefinitely. It simply needs advanced memory to remain essential to the broader AI ecosystem.
While AI-driven growth has fueled substantial earnings expansion for SK Hynix, the company's valuation remains fairly modest on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis.

The company's leadership in the HBM market and progress in new chip technology give SK Hynix strong competitive advantages that extend beyond today's memory supercycle. When combined with its attractive valuation profile, I view SK Hynix as a compelling long-term buy for investors seeking exposure to the AI infrastructure boom.

Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » During downturns, I prefer companies with established competitive advantages , diversified revenue streams, and enough financial flexibility to keep investing while weaker competitors fall behind. This is why Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is near the top of my shopping list. One of Alphabet's biggest strengths is that so many of its products are embedded in everyday life. Think about how frequently people use Google Search, Gmail, YouTube, Google Maps, Android, and Chrome. Although the use of these services isn't a discretionary purchase in the traditional sense, they are integrated into how billions of people around the world communicate, navigate, work, and discover information. The advantage of this model is that Alphabet can attract users through its ecosystem of free services and monetize people's activity through advertising. Since its products are interconnected, Alphabet can easily introduce new features and services to existing customers rather than constantly creating new products and marketing to different demographics. Alphabet's reach extends far beyond consumers. Through Google Cloud, Alphabet provides computing infrastructure, cybersecurity, data analytics, and AI services to enterprise customers. This diversified business model comes in handy during economic downturns. Advertising budgets often decline when businesses become cautious, but enterprise technology budgets usually follow different priorities. The most compelling thing about Alphabet is the company's ability to vertically integrate its various businesses. Within Google Cloud, the company offers its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also operates data centers, builds AI models through Google DeepMind, and distributes AI-powered products through Search, Gemini, and Workspace. During the 2008 financial crisis, Alphabet shares declined 55% for the year. The recession pressured advertising spending, and investors abandoned growth stocks. The stock also experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of roughly 31% during the COVID-19 crash in early 2020. Most recently, Alphabet lost roughly 39% of its value during the 2022 bear market as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty dragged on the technology sector. While those are substantial losses, here's what makes Alphabet interesting. Despite experiencing multiple severe downturns, the company continued growing its businesses, launching new products, and quietly strengthening its competitive position. The gray-shaded columns in the chart below mark recessions. The theme here is that investors who bought Alphabet stock during market downturns and held on to their positions benefited materially from the company's subsequent recoveries. During the second quarter, Alphabet generated $119.8 billion in revenue, representing 24% growth year over year. Its Google Services segment generated $94.5 billion in revenue while Google Cloud grew an impressive 82% to $24.8 billion. This shows how Alphabet is able to benefit from both an established advertising franchise and the AI economy. The real story is that Alphabet generated $39.1 billion in operating cash flow during the second quarter, giving the company substantial financial resources to fund research, infrastructure, and other investments. The company ended June with $242.5 billion in cash and marketable securities. Alphabet's financial flexibility gives the company the ability to invest in AI infrastructure, develop new products, pursue acquisitions, and maintain shareholder distributions (i.e., dividends) without depending entirely on outside financing. Against this backdrop, Alphabet stock could still fall substantially if the market crashes. Nevertheless, history suggests the company's diversified ecosystem, vertical integration, and extraordinary financial horsepower put Alphabet in a good position to endure a downturn and emerge even stronger. Rather than attempting to time the next stock market crash, I'd consider buying Alphabet stock gradually over time during dips and holding it for the long term. The most compelling thing about Alphabet is the company's ability to vertically integrate its various businesses. Within Google Cloud, the company offers its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also operates data centers, builds AI models through Google DeepMind, and distributes AI-powered products through Search, Gemini, and Workspace.

During the 2008 financial crisis, Alphabet shares declined 55% for the year. The recession pressured advertising spending, and investors abandoned growth stocks. The stock also experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of roughly 31% during the COVID-19 crash in early 2020. Most recently, Alphabet lost roughly 39% of its value during the 2022 bear market as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty dragged on the technology sector.

While those are substantial losses, here's what makes Alphabet interesting. Despite experiencing multiple severe downturns, the company continued growing its businesses, launching new products, and quietly strengthening its competitive position. The gray-shaded columns in the chart below mark recessions. The theme here is that investors who bought Alphabet stock during market downturns and held on to their positions benefited materially from the company's subsequent recoveries.

During the second quarter, Alphabet generated $119.8 billion in revenue, representing 24% growth year over year. Its Google Services segment generated $94.5 billion in revenue while Google Cloud grew an impressive 82% to $24.8 billion. This shows how Alphabet is able to benefit from both an established advertising franchise and the AI economy.

The real story is that Alphabet generated $39.1 billion in operating cash flow during the second quarter, giving the company substantial financial resources to fund research, infrastructure, and other investments. The company ended June with $242.5 billion in cash and marketable securities.

Alphabet's financial flexibility gives the company the ability to invest in AI infrastructure, develop new products, pursue acquisitions, and maintain shareholder distributions (i.e., dividends) without depending entirely on outside financing.

Against this backdrop, Alphabet stock could still fall substantially if the market crashes. Nevertheless, history suggests the company's diversified ecosystem, vertical integration, and extraordinary financial horsepower put Alphabet in a good position to endure a downturn and emerge even stronger. Rather than attempting to time the next stock market crash, I'd consider buying Alphabet stock gradually over time during dips and holding it for the long term.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been one of the biggest drivers of the stock market's rally over the last few years. While this enthusiasm has propelled the S&P 500 to record highs, there's a growing concern that investors may be getting ahead of themselves.

The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio , which measures stock valuations against 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings, is hovering above 41. After several years of exceptional returns, investors should think about what stocks they want to own if sentiment suddenly changes.

During downturns, I prefer companies with established competitive advantages , diversified revenue streams, and enough financial flexibility to keep investing while weaker competitors fall behind. This is why Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is near the top of my shopping list.

One of Alphabet's biggest strengths is that so many of its products are embedded in everyday life. Think about how frequently people use Google Search, Gmail, YouTube, Google Maps, Android, and Chrome. Although the use of these services isn't a discretionary purchase in the traditional sense, they are integrated into how billions of people around the world communicate, navigate, work, and discover information.

The advantage of this model is that Alphabet can attract users through its ecosystem of free services and monetize people's activity through advertising. Since its products are interconnected, Alphabet can easily introduce new features and services to existing customers rather than constantly creating new products and marketing to different demographics.

Alphabet's reach extends far beyond consumers. Through Google Cloud, Alphabet provides computing infrastructure, cybersecurity, data analytics, and AI services to enterprise customers. This diversified business model comes in handy during economic downturns. Advertising budgets often decline when businesses become cautious, but enterprise technology budgets usually follow different priorities.

The most compelling thing about Alphabet is the company's ability to vertically integrate its various businesses. Within Google Cloud, the company offers its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also operates data centers, builds AI models through Google DeepMind, and distributes AI-powered products through Search, Gemini, and Workspace.

During the 2008 financial crisis, Alphabet shares declined 55% for the year. The recession pressured advertising spending, and investors abandoned growth stocks. The stock also experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of roughly 31% during the COVID-19 crash in early 2020. Most recently, Alphabet lost roughly 39% of its value during the 2022 bear market as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty dragged on the technology sector.

While those are substantial losses, here's what makes Alphabet interesting. Despite experiencing multiple severe downturns, the company continued growing its businesses, launching new products, and quietly strengthening its competitive position. The gray-shaded columns in the chart below mark recessions. The theme here is that investors who bought Alphabet stock during market downturns and held on to their positions benefited materially from the company's subsequent recoveries.

During the second quarter, Alphabet generated $119.8 billion in revenue, representing 24% growth year over year. Its Google Services segment generated $94.5 billion in revenue while Google Cloud grew an impressive 82% to $24.8 billion. This shows how Alphabet is able to benefit from both an established advertising franchise and the AI economy.

The real story is that Alphabet generated $39.1 billion in operating cash flow during the second quarter, giving the company substantial financial resources to fund research, infrastructure, and other investments. The company ended June with $242.5 billion in cash and marketable securities.

Alphabet's financial flexibility gives the company the ability to invest in AI infrastructure, develop new products, pursue acquisitions, and maintain shareholder distributions (i.e., dividends) without depending entirely on outside financing.

Against this backdrop, Alphabet stock could still fall substantially if the market crashes. Nevertheless, history suggests the company's diversified ecosystem, vertical integration, and extraordinary financial horsepower put Alphabet in a good position to endure a downturn and emerge even stronger. I'm doing it right now, and if Iren stays at such a low price, I will intensify my buying. The company has several bullish catalysts, and certain "bearish" claims about Iren and the neocloud industry are actually quite bullish for Iren on closer inspection.

Almost all the bearish concerns people bring up about Iren are actually bullish. First, Gartner released research that projected 80% of neoclouds ceasing independent operations by 2030 while casting doubts about AI infrastructure spending.

However, Iren remains one of the top neocloud providers and has a pristine balance sheet. If 80% of neocloud providers are out of business by 2030, Iren's capacity will become much more valuable due to supply constraints.

Second, CoreWeave 's ( CRWV -11.91% ) corporate bonds reached yields of 15%, causing investors to worry about how expensive it would be for neoclouds to borrow money in the future. However, CoreWeave has an elevated rate because its balance sheet is under duress. CoreWeave has a current ratio of 0.46 and will need to refinance some of its debt. Iren has a much more favorable current ratio of 3.55.

MARA hasn’t explained these transfers. So, is MARA selling Bitcoin?

In contrast, Michael Saylor, executive chairman of Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ), signaled more Bitcoin purchases. He tweeted, “We found room for more orange,” his usual hint at another purchase. Strategy Inc. holds 848,250 BTC and last reported buying 250 BTC, though it has not made a new announcement yet.
Bitcoin trades at approximately $82,720. MARA shares were at $7.70 premarket, up 2.3% from the previous close of $7.53, even though they remain down 20.2% for the week and 30.3% for the month.
Meanwhile, Strategy Inc. was trading at around $140 premarket, down 9.6% for the week, as investors worry that a stock index could drop the company.

MARA primarily earns revenue through Bitcoin mining, where specialized computers compete to add new blocks to the network and earn newly mined coins. Its revenue decreased to $174.9 million in the second quarter, down from $238.5 million the previous year. A 28% drop in Bitcoin’s average price cut revenue by $65.9 million.

MARA’s hashrate, the total computing power its machines contribute to the network, rose to 70.3 exahashes per second. However, the cost of energy needed to mine each Bitcoin has increased to $38,690 from $33,735 a year ago. Management attributed this rise to increased mining difficulty, which occurs when more machines come online.

About $343 million of MARA’s $611.3 million net loss came from a mark-to-market loss, which is a paper loss from valuing its Bitcoin at lower prices without selling any coins. Management noted that every $10,000 change in Bitcoin’s price affects that line by approximately $350 million. MARA ended the quarter with $421.3 million in cash.

MARA is also moving into energy and is acquiring Long Ridge Energy, a gas-fired power plant, in a $1.5 billion deal, including debt. MARA plans to assume about $900 million of Long Ridge’s debt, and the deal is pending approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).

MARA has also secured rights to a 2 GW-powered site in Matagorda County, Texas, with plans to convert most of its capacity for AI and high-performance computing through a joint venture with Starwood. Its Exaion unit already operates an AI cloud in Europe, ensuring customer data complies with European regulations. We also cover seven suppliers benefiting from similar shifts in a free AI infrastructure report .

To finance these ventures, MARA borrowed $600 million using Bitcoin-backed credit facilities with Coinbase ( NASDAQ:COIN ) and Two Prime at an average interest rate of 7.6%. Lenders can claim the pledged Bitcoin if MARA fails to repay, and the new loans left 54% of MARA’s Bitcoin pledged as collateral.

Management has indicated that MARA will continue to sell Bitcoin selectively to fund operations. Its filings support this, showing MARA held 35,577 BTC at the end of June, down from 49,951 BTC a year earlier, with no updated figures released since its August 6 earnings call.

Companies that send coins to an exchange are often preparing to sell, as exchanges facilitate trades between buyers and sellers. However, companies also move coins for other reasons, like lending them out, using them as collateral, or hedging against price fluctuations . MARA does engage in lending; in the second quarter, it had 4,742 BTC out on loan, generating about $4.3 million in interest.

While the deposits may imply a sale, they don’t prove one. MARA reported Coinbase and Two Prime as lenders for the new credit lines, yet the coins were sent to Binance and Gate. MARA has not disclosed any specific buyers, sale prices, or proceeds, and it hasn’t confirmed the wallet labels Lookonchain assigned.

Saylor’s tweet also warrants close examination. As the head of the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, he promotes the asset central to his company’s balance sheet, but his post mentions no specific amounts, dates, or funding sources. Strategy Inc. has also sold Bitcoin this year, with $218.4 million sold to date under its Bitcoin monetization program as of its second-quarter report.

During the same period as Strategy Inc.’s last 250 BTC purchase, the company also spent $192.4 million buying back preferred shares instead of buying more Bitcoin. MARA’s deposit of 1,000 BTC is four times that 250 BTC buy.

Signs suggest MARA may be selling, or preparing to sell, some of its Bitcoin. The coins went to trading platforms, and MARA has said it sells Bitcoin selectively. It also has a power plant deal, AI expansion plans, and rising mining costs to fund. Selling Bitcoin can generate cash without diluting shareholders, but it may weigh slightly on Bitcoin prices since the proceeds go into infrastructure.

MARA’s next update should settle it. If the report shows fewer than 35,577 BTC and mentions any sales, the coins were sold; steady holdings, with more coins lent or pledged, would suggest a collateral move. An 8-K filing showing Strategy Inc. buying more than 1,000 BTC would mean one buyer absorbed the miner’s coins. MARA’s shares could still rise on FERC approval or new leases, even if Bitcoin prices stall.

extraction.body: XRP's (XRP) spot market activity is fading across two key trading venues even as traders gradually increase leveraged positions in derivatives markets. Trading volumes on South Korea's Upbit have been declining, while spot deposits and withdrawals on Binance have nearly stalled. At the same time, Open Interest continues to rise despite subdued funding rates, suggesting traders are adding exposure cautiously rather than aggressively chasing price. XRP is trading around 1,655 won on Upbit, but market participation has steadily weakened. Weekly trading volume has declined for four consecutive weeks, falling from roughly 530 million XRP in late June to 258 million by mid-July. That represents a drop of nearly 51% in just one month. The decline points to weaker trading activity and suggests local investor participation has cooled. Despite the slowdown, XRP remains Upbit's second-largest trading market behind Bitcoin (BTC). However, the token is currently trading about 1.1% below its global fair value. The disappearance of the Kimchi premium, a price premium that has historically reflected strong retail demand in South Korea, further points to declining local interest in XRP. The slowdown is also evident on Binance. According to on-chain analyst CryptoOnchain, XRP exchange-based inflows and outflows both plunged by roughly 99% over the past week. Meanwhile, on Binance, the number of deposit addresses fell 97.6% compared with the weekly average. The sharp contraction suggests significantly fewer users are transferring XRP onto or off the exchange. While this does not necessarily indicate selling pressure, it does point to a broader decline in spot market participation as traders remain on the sidelines. While spot activity is fading, derivatives markets are telling a different story. XRP Open Interest increased 5.9% to 423.8 million on Binance, pushing the estimated leverage ratio up to 0.162, its highest reading in recent weeks. Meanwhile, funding rates remained close to neutral and fell 29.9% from the previous week. Even so, they still sit 172.5% above their monthly average and 271.7% above their quarterly baseline. "This suggests the leverage build isn't being driven by aggressive one-sided speculation, but rather a slow repositioning process occurring largely without spot participants at the table," CryptoOnchain noted. The cautious picture extends beyond derivatives. XRP's Network Value to Transactions (NVT) ratio has climbed 45.6% above its three-month baseline, while transaction counts have fallen 33.6% and active addresses are down 16.4%. Together, these metrics suggest network usage is weakening even as market participants build derivatives exposure. The data comes as XRP has posted modest gains over the past week, benefiting from the broader cryptocurrency market rally. The token traded at $1.13, up 3.96% over the past day. However, the recovery is occurring amid weakening spot participation. While collapsing exchange flows can sometimes reflect investors moving assets into cold storage or exchange-traded products rather than actively selling, they also indicate a lack of fresh spot buying entering the market. The divergence suggests derivatives positioning is playing a larger role in recent price action than spot activity. Whether the rally proves durable may depend on whether spot demand begins to recover. As of October 18, XRP is priced at $1.31, down 7.1% over the past week and 13.5% over the previous two weeks, leaving it 64% below its peak of $3.65. This raises the question: Is South Korea still XRP’s biggest market, or did XRP only secure the top spot in a shrinking pool? Trading volume reflects the total value of all trades an exchange executes during a specific period. Upbit ranks cryptocurrencies by this value, so when XRP ranks first, it means more won changed hands in XRP than in Bitcoin or Tether. However, remember that every transaction has a buyer and a seller, so the 8.35 trillion won figure includes both buying and selling activity. Volume alone does not reveal which side was more active. Traders closely monitor these rankings because Korean retail investors have long preferred XRP. Many of these traders operate on Upbit’s won pairs. When XRP ranks first, it often signals renewed demand from Korea. This interpretation is more reliable when Upbit’s overall trading volume also rises, indicating that new investment capital is entering the market. Despite XRP holding the top position on Upbit, the exchange’s total trading volume fell 15.5% during the same week. Rankings reflect market share, so a coin’s share can rise even as overall trading activity declines. So, XRP at the top during a period of decreased activity might suggest Korean traders kept focusing on XRP while trading in other coins slowed, indicating loyalty rather than new demand. Although Upbit outperformed the broader market, where overall trading volume fell 19.6%, it still reported lower trading than the previous week. Two key metrics remain undisclosed for this week: XRP’s precise share of Upbit’s total volume and the proportion of global XRP trading conducted in Korean won. Without this information, analysts cannot determine how much of XRP’s worldwide trading volume is attributable to Korea versus dollar pairs on other exchanges. XRP’s 7.1% drop over the same week it led Upbit adds uncertainty to the data, as high trading volume during a price decline could indicate sellers accepting offers just as easily as buyers entering the market. On dollar markets, XRP hit a low of $1.25 on October 18, its lowest daily low in the past month. Market makers also impact exchange volume. These firms place buy and sell orders on both sides of the order book and profit from the spread, so their transactions can inflate volume figures without changing who actually holds XRP. XRP’s price movements largely depend on fresh investment and sustained buying interest. U.S. spot XRP ETFs offer clear insight into this investment flow, and recently, that flow has slowed. Data from SoSoValue shows a net outflow of $2.5 million on October 16, a smaller outflow of about $105,000 on October 15, and no net flow on several days earlier in the month. In contrast, ETF inflows were notably different in late September. On September 25, these funds recorded a net inflow of $22.6 million, their largest intake in the past month, during the same buying run that took XRP to an intraday high of $1.66 on September 23. Unfortunately, ETF holders are currently at a loss. Total net assets sat at $1.47 billion on October 16, below the cumulative $1.80 billion in inflows. Holders often sell during rallies to recoup losses, which could limit potential price rebounds. South Korean interest hasn’t shielded XRP from this year’s price declines. XRP has fallen 29.1% year-to-date, compared to Bitcoin’s 6.2% drop, Ethereum ‘s ( CRYPTO: ETH ) 18.9% decline, and Solana ‘s ( CRYPTO: SOL ) 16.5% reduction. South Korea remains XRP’s most loyal retail market, as Upbit’s rankings indicate. However, this ranking alone cannot definitively prove Korea is XRP’s biggest market or reveal new demand, especially considering XRP’s top position occurred during a week of declining overall volume. Fully answering this question would require better insights into the won’s share of global XRP trading. The first test is volume. If Upbit’s next weekly report shows total volume back above 8.35 trillion won with XRP still on top, fresh won could be flowing into XRP, while a smaller total would mean fewer Korean traders. The second test is price. XRP needs to hold its $1.25 low and recover the $1.41 October 11 close; a daily close below $1.25 would show Korean trading isn’t providing support.
