extraction.body: XRP's (XRP) spot market activity is fading across two key trading venues even as traders gradually increase leveraged positions in derivatives markets. Trading volumes on South Korea's Upbit have been declining, while spot deposits and withdrawals on Binance have nearly stalled. At the same time, Open Interest continues to rise despite subdued funding rates, suggesting traders are adding exposure cautiously rather than aggressively chasing price. XRP is trading around 1,655 won on Upbit, but market participation has steadily weakened. Weekly trading volume has declined for four consecutive weeks, falling from roughly 530 million XRP in late June to 258 million by mid-July. That represents a drop of nearly 51% in just one month. The decline points to weaker trading activity and suggests local investor participation has cooled. Despite the slowdown, XRP remains Upbit's second-largest trading market behind Bitcoin (BTC). However, the token is currently trading about 1.1% below its global fair value. The disappearance of the Kimchi premium, a price premium that has historically reflected strong retail demand in South Korea, further points to declining local interest in XRP. The slowdown is also evident on Binance. According to on-chain analyst CryptoOnchain, XRP exchange-based inflows and outflows both plunged by roughly 99% over the past week. Meanwhile, on Binance, the number of deposit addresses fell 97.6% compared with the weekly average. The sharp contraction suggests significantly fewer users are transferring XRP onto or off the exchange. While this does not necessarily indicate selling pressure, it does point to a broader decline in spot market participation as traders remain on the sidelines. While spot activity is fading, derivatives markets are telling a different story. XRP Open Interest increased 5.9% to 423.8 million on Binance, pushing the estimated leverage ratio up to 0.162, its highest reading in recent weeks. Meanwhile, funding rates remained close to neutral and fell 29.9% from the previous week. Even so, they still sit 172.5% above their monthly average and 271.7% above their quarterly baseline. "This suggests the leverage build isn't being driven by aggressive one-sided speculation, but rather a slow repositioning process occurring largely without spot participants at the table," CryptoOnchain noted. The cautious picture extends beyond derivatives. XRP's Network Value to Transactions (NVT) ratio has climbed 45.6% above its three-month baseline, while transaction counts have fallen 33.6% and active addresses are down 16.4%. Together, these metrics suggest network usage is weakening even as market participants build derivatives exposure. The data comes as XRP has posted modest gains over the past week, benefiting from the broader cryptocurrency market rally. The token traded at $1.13, up 3.96% over the past day. However, the recovery is occurring amid weakening spot participation. While collapsing exchange flows can sometimes reflect investors moving assets into cold storage or exchange-traded products rather than actively selling, they also indicate a lack of fresh spot buying entering the market. The divergence suggests derivatives positioning is playing a larger role in recent price action than spot activity. Whether the rally proves durable may depend on whether spot demand begins to recover. extraction.body: XRP claimed the top trading spot on South Korea's largest exchange, but a shrinking market and falling price cloud what that ranking actually means for the token's future. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) emerged as the most-traded coin on Upbit, South Korea’s largest crypto exchange, for the week ending October 18, 2026. It led Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) and Tether ( CRYPTO: USDT ), the widely used stablecoin . Despite this achievement, XRP’s top position came during a sluggish trading week. Upbit recorded total trading volume of 8.35 trillion won (approximately $6.28 billion), down 15.5% from the previous week. Overall trading volume across major exchanges fell 19.6%. Korean traders have shown little new buying interest in XRP. As of October 18, XRP is priced at $1.31, down 7.1% over the past week and 13.5% over the previous two weeks, leaving it 64% below its peak of $3.65. This raises the question: Is South Korea still XRP’s biggest market, or did XRP only secure the top spot in a shrinking pool? Trading volume reflects the total value of all trades an exchange executes during a specific period. Upbit ranks cryptocurrencies by this value, so when XRP ranks first, it means more won changed hands in XRP than in Bitcoin or Tether. However, remember that every transaction has a buyer and a seller, so the 8.35 trillion won figure includes both buying and selling activity. Volume alone does not reveal which side was more active. Traders closely monitor these rankings because Korean retail investors have long preferred XRP. Many of these traders operate on Upbit’s won pairs. When XRP ranks first, it often signals renewed demand from Korea. This interpretation is more reliable when Upbit’s overall trading volume also rises, indicating that new investment capital is entering the market. Despite XRP holding the top position on Upbit, the exchange’s total trading volume fell 15.5% during the same week. Rankings reflect market share, so a coin’s share can rise even as overall trading activity declines. So, XRP at the top during a period of decreased activity might suggest Korean traders kept focusing on XRP while trading in other coins slowed, indicating loyalty rather than new demand. Although Upbit outperformed the broader market, where overall trading volume fell 19.6%, it still reported lower trading than the previous week. Two key metrics remain undisclosed for this week: XRP’s precise share of Upbit’s total volume and the proportion of global XRP trading conducted in Korean won. Without this information, analysts cannot determine how much of XRP’s worldwide trading volume is attributable to Korea versus dollar pairs on other exchanges. XRP’s 7.1% drop over the same week it led Upbit adds uncertainty to the data, as high trading volume during a price decline could indicate sellers accepting offers just as easily as buyers entering the market. On dollar markets, XRP hit a low of $1.25 on October 18, its lowest daily low in the past month. Market makers also impact exchange volume. These firms place buy and sell orders on both sides of the order book and profit from the spread, so their transactions can inflate volume figures without changing who actually holds XRP. XRP’s price movements largely depend on fresh investment and sustained buying interest. U.S. spot XRP ETFs offer clear insight into this investment flow, and recently, that flow has slowed. Data from SoSoValue shows a net outflow of $2.5 million on October 16, a smaller outflow of about $105,000 on October 15, and no net flow on several days earlier in the month. In contrast, ETF inflows were notably different in late September. On September 25, these funds recorded a net inflow of $22.6 million, their largest intake in the past month, during the same buying run that took XRP to an intraday high of $1.66 on September 23. Unfortunately, ETF holders are currently at a loss. Total net assets sat at $1.47 billion on October 16, below the cumulative $1.80 billion in inflows. Holders often sell during rallies to recoup losses, which could limit potential price rebounds. South Korean interest hasn’t shielded XRP from this year’s price declines. XRP has fallen 29.1% year-to-date, compared to Bitcoin’s 6.2% drop, Ethereum ‘s ( CRYPTO: ETH ) 18.9% decline, and Solana ‘s ( CRYPTO: SOL ) 16.5% reduction. South Korea remains XRP’s most loyal retail market, as Upbit’s rankings indicate. However, this ranking alone cannot definitively prove Korea is XRP’s biggest market or reveal new demand, especially considering XRP’s top position occurred during a week of declining overall volume. Fully answering this question would require better insights into the won’s share of global XRP trading. The first test is volume. If Upbit’s next weekly report shows total volume back above 8.35 trillion won with XRP still on top, fresh won could be flowing into XRP, while a smaller total would mean fewer Korean traders. The second test is price. XRP needs to hold its $1.25 low and recover the $1.41 October 11 close; a daily close below $1.25 would show Korean trading isn’t providing support. passages: In its latest Bitcoin and Solana price prediction, Claude, the AI model developed by Anthropic, predicts that Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) could reach $240,000 and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) might reach $320 by the end of 2030.
These predictions start from prices of about $82,810 for Bitcoin and $106 for Solana, where both coins traded when Claude made the forecast.
Strategy Inc. selling Bitcoin after November 30 would hurt Bitcoin's chances, while positive Solana ETF flows would make Solana's 2030 target far more credible.
If given $5,000 to invest, Claude would allocate $3,500 to Bitcoin and $1,500 to Solana, balancing each investment based on potential price declines.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Both cryptocurrencies have rebounded, with Bitcoin up 23.4% and Solana increasing by 33% over the last 90 days.
Solana, on the other hand, faces more challenges in reaching the $320 target.
For Bitcoin, achieving the goal depends on stabilizing corporate buying trends, boosting ETF flows, and surpassing its previous record of $126,080.
For Solana, success hinges on the Alpenglow upgrade's effectiveness and on becoming a go-to choice for stablecoin and tokenization projects.
Claude's price target for Bitcoin ranges from $150,000 to $400,000.
Unlike Bitcoin, Solana does not have a maximum supply, and its total supply of more than 636 million tokens already tops the 589 million in circulation.

The upcoming Alpenglow upgrade, scheduled for activation on October 21, aims to cut transaction finality, the point after which a transaction can't be reversed, to 150 milliseconds, which Claude says makes Solana's settlement pitch technically credible.
After years of waiting for a good option, SoFi now offers access to major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana, along with more than 25 total digital assets.
Bitcoin gets a 60% chance of a new all-time high by 2027, while Solana gets only 30%, weighed down by a $70 downside floor.

In its latest Bitcoin and Solana price prediction, Claude, the AI model developed by Anthropic, predicts that Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) could reach $240,000 and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) might reach $320 by the end of 2030. These predictions start from prices of about $82,810 for Bitcoin and $106 for Solana, where both coins traded when Claude made the forecast. Bitcoin is trading at about $82,720, which is 34.4% lower than its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025. In comparison, Solana trades at around $106, which is 64% below its peak of $293 from January 2025. Both cryptocurrencies have rebounded, with Bitcoin up 23.4% and Solana increasing by 33% over the last 90 days. However, Solana experienced a slight decline of 5.6% over the past month. So, which cryptocurrency stands a better chance of hitting Claude's targets? Claude's price target for Bitcoin ranges from $150,000 to $400,000. The lower end assumes a lackluster market after the scheduled Bitcoin halving in April 2028, which cuts miners' rewards. This scenario also considers pressure from corporate treasuries, companies that borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin and could weigh on the market. The higher target assumes a strong post-halving rally and increased interest from institutional investors through exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Achieving the $240,000 target would represent a return of 189.8%, roughly 29% per year. As Bitcoin's supply is nearly capped at 21 million coins, with 20,098,843 already mined, any price increase will largely depend on new buyers entering the market. For Solana, the forecast is broader, ranging from $70 to $700. The $320 target represents a 202.6% return and is 9% above Solana's previous record. Unlike Bitcoin, Solana does not have a maximum supply, and its total supply of more than 636 million tokens already tops the 589 million in circulation. Hence, Solana would need to achieve a market value higher than its previous all-time high to reach this price point. Claude gives Bitcoin a 60% chance of reaching a new all-time high by the end of 2027, which would require a 52% gain from current levels. In contrast, Claude gives Solana a 30% chance of breaking its previous record, which would need a substantial 177% increase. Bitcoin's price predictions depend heavily on demand for Bitcoin ETFs, which directly hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. As of October 16, these ETFs held approximately $104.3 billion in net assets. However, investors have withdrawn a net total of $617.2 million from them in October through that date. For Claude's higher price forecast to materialize, this trend needs to reverse and turn into consistent buying. Bitcoin also faces risks, particularly from significant corporate treasury sales. For example, Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) holds about 848,250 BTC, or roughly 4% of the total supply, and new MSCI index rules could cost it billions in passive holdings by index funds. If MSCI excludes Strategy from its indexes starting November 30, demand for its shares could fall, potentially prompting Bitcoin selling as ETF demand wanes. For Solana to reach the high end of its forecast at $700, it must become the primary settlement layer for stablecoins (dollar-pegged tokens) and tokenized assets like stocks and bonds on the blockchain. The upcoming Alpenglow upgrade, scheduled for activation on October 21, aims to cut transaction finality, the point after which a transaction can't be reversed, to 150 milliseconds, which Claude says makes Solana's settlement pitch technically credible. However, the upgrade's success depends on network revenue growing with it. The main risk is that technological advancement could outpace demand if stablecoin issuers and tokenization projects continue to favor Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH). If given $5,000 to invest, Claude would allocate $3,500 to Bitcoin and $1,500 to Solana, balancing each investment based on potential price declines. For investors with a higher risk tolerance and the ability to withstand greater market fluctuations, Claude suggests a 60/40 split. While Solana's projected return slightly exceeds Bitcoin's by 13 percentage points — 202.6% versus 189.8% — Claude notes that when factoring in probability-weighted expected returns, the outcomes appear more even. This is largely because Solana's $70 price floor is lower than its current trading level. Overall, we believe Bitcoin has a fair chance of reaching $240,000 by the end of 2030. Solana, on the other hand, faces more challenges in reaching the $320 target. For Bitcoin, achieving the goal depends on stabilizing corporate buying trends, boosting ETF flows, and surpassing its previous record of $126,080. For Solana, success hinges on the Alpenglow upgrade's effectiveness and on becoming a go-to choice for stablecoin and tokenization projects. Both forecasts carry a downside. If the corporate treasury trade unwinds, Claude's $150,000 floor looks more realistic for Bitcoin, and if demand stays on Ethereum, Solana could drift toward $70. Strategy Inc. selling Bitcoin after November 30 would hurt Bitcoin's chances, while positive Solana ETF flows would make Solana's 2030 target far more credible. In its latest Bitcoin and Solana price prediction, Claude, the AI model developed by Anthropic, predicts that Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) could reach $240,000 and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) might reach $320 by the end of 2030. These predictions start from prices of about $82,810 for Bitcoin and $106 for Solana, where both coins traded when Claude made the forecast.

Bitcoin is trading at about $82,720, which is 34.4% lower than its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025. In comparison, Solana trades at around $106, which is 64% below its peak of $293 from January 2025.

Both cryptocurrencies have rebounded, with Bitcoin up 23.4% and Solana increasing by 33% over the last 90 days. However, Solana experienced a slight decline of 5.6% over the past month. So, which cryptocurrency stands a better chance of hitting Claude's targets?

Claude's price target for Bitcoin ranges from $150,000 to $400,000. The lower end assumes a lackluster market after the scheduled Bitcoin halving in April 2028, which cuts miners' rewards. This scenario also considers pressure from corporate treasuries, companies that borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin and could weigh on the market. The higher target assumes a strong post-halving rally and increased interest from institutional investors through exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

Achieving the $240,000 target would represent a return of 189.8%, roughly 29% per year. As Bitcoin's supply is nearly capped at 21 million coins, with 20,098,843 already mined, any price increase will largely depend on new buyers entering the market.

For Solana, the forecast is broader, ranging from $70 to $700. The $320 target represents a 202.6% return and is 9% above Solana's previous record. Unlike Bitcoin, Solana does not have a maximum supply, and its total supply of more than 636 million tokens already tops the 589 million in circulation. Hence, Solana would need to achieve a market value higher than its previous all-time high to reach this price point.

Claude gives Bitcoin a 60% chance of reaching a new all-time high by the end of 2027, which would require a 52% gain from current levels. In contrast, Claude gives Solana a 30% chance of breaking its previous record, which would need a substantial 177% increase.

Bitcoin's price predictions depend heavily on demand for Bitcoin ETFs, which directly hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. As of October 16, these ETFs held approximately $104.3 billion in net assets. However, investors have withdrawn a net total of $617.2 million from them in October through that date. For Claude's higher price forecast to materialize, this trend needs to reverse and turn into consistent buying.

Bitcoin also faces risks, particularly from significant corporate treasury sales. For example, Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) holds about 848,250 BTC, or roughly 4% of the total supply, and new MSCI index rules could cost it billions in passive holdings by index funds. If MSCI excludes Strategy from its indexes starting November 30, demand for its shares could fall, potentially prompting Bitcoin selling as ETF demand wanes.

For Solana to reach the high end of its forecast at $700, it must become the primary settlement layer for stablecoins (dollar-pegged tokens) and tokenized assets like stocks and bonds on the blockchain. The upcoming Alpenglow upgrade, scheduled for activation on October 21, aims to cut transaction finality, the point after which a transaction can't be reversed, to 150 milliseconds, which Claude says makes Solana's settlement pitch technically credible.

However, the upgrade's success depends on network revenue growing with it. The main risk is that technological advancement could outpace demand if stablecoin issuers and tokenization projects continue to favor Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH).

If given $5,000 to invest, Claude would allocate $3,500 to Bitcoin and $1,500 to Solana, balancing each investment based on potential price declines. For investors with a higher risk tolerance and the ability to withstand greater market fluctuations, Claude suggests a 60/40 split.

While Solana's projected return slightly exceeds Bitcoin's by 13 percentage points — 202.6% versus 189.8% — Claude notes that when factoring in probability-weighted expected returns, the outcomes appear more even. This is largely because Solana's $70 price floor is lower than its current trading level.

Overall, we believe Bitcoin has a fair chance of reaching $240,000 by the end of 2030. Solana, on the other hand, faces more challenges in reaching the $320 target. For Bitcoin, achieving the goal depends on stabilizing corporate buying trends, boosting ETF flows, and surpassing its previous record of $126,080. For Solana, success hinges on the Alpenglow upgrade's effectiveness and on becoming a go-to choice for stablecoin and tokenization projects.

Both forecasts carry a downside. If the corporate treasury trade unwinds, Claude's $150,000 floor looks more realistic for Bitcoin, and if demand stays on Ethereum, Solana could drift toward $70. Strategy Inc. selling Bitcoin after November 30 would hurt Bitcoin's chances, while positive Solana ETF flows would make Solana's 2030 target far more credible.

These predictions start from prices of about $82,810 for Bitcoin and $106 for Solana, where both coins traded when Claude made the forecast.

Bitcoin is trading at about $82,720, which is 34.4% lower than its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025. In comparison, Solana trades at around $106, which is 64% below its peak of $293 from January 2025.

Both cryptocurrencies have rebounded, with Bitcoin up 23.4% and Solana increasing by 33% over the last 90 days. However, Solana experienced a slight decline of 5.6% over the past month. So, which cryptocurrency stands a better chance of hitting Claude’s targets?

Claude’s price target for Bitcoin ranges from $150,000 to $400,000. The lower end assumes a lackluster market after the scheduled Bitcoin halving in April 2028, which cuts miners’ rewards. This scenario also considers pressure from corporate treasuries, companies that borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin and could weigh on the market. The higher target assumes a strong post-halving rally and increased interest from institutional investors through exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

Achieving the $240,000 target would represent a return of 189.8%, roughly 29% per year. As Bitcoin’s supply is nearly capped at 21 million coins, with 20,098,843 already mined, any price increase will largely depend on new buyers entering the market.

For Solana, the forecast is broader, ranging from $70 to $700. The $320 target represents a 202.6% return and is 9% above Solana’s previous record. Unlike Bitcoin, Solana does not have a maximum supply, and its total supply of more than 636 million tokens already tops the 589 million in circulation. Hence, Solana would need to achieve a market value higher than its previous all-time high to reach this price point.

Claude gives Bitcoin a 60% chance of reaching a new all-time high by the end of 2027, which would require a 52% gain from current levels. In contrast, Claude gives Solana a 30% chance of breaking its previous record, which would need a substantial 177% increase.

Bitcoin’s price predictions depend heavily on demand for Bitcoin ETFs, which directly hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. As of October 16, these ETFs held approximately $104.3 billion in net assets. However, investors have withdrawn a net total of $617.2 million from them in October through that date. For Claude’s higher price forecast to materialize, this trend needs to reverse and turn into consistent buying .

Bitcoin also faces risks, particularly from significant corporate treasury sales. For example, Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ) holds about 848,250 BTC, or roughly 4% of the total supply, and new MSCI index rules could cost it billions in passive holdings by index funds. If MSCI excludes Strategy from its indexes starting November 30, demand for its shares could fall, potentially prompting Bitcoin selling as ETF demand wanes.

For Solana to reach the high end of its forecast at $700, it must become the primary settlement layer for stablecoins (dollar-pegged tokens) and tokenized assets like stocks and bonds on the blockchain. The upcoming Alpenglow upgrade , scheduled for activation on October 21, aims to cut transaction finality, the point after which a transaction can’t be reversed, to 150 milliseconds, which Claude says makes Solana’s settlement pitch technically credible.

However, the upgrade’s success depends on network revenue growing with it. The main risk is that technological advancement could outpace demand if stablecoin issuers and tokenization projects continue to favor Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ).

If given $5,000 to invest, Claude would allocate $3,500 to Bitcoin and $1,500 to Solana, balancing each investment based on potential price declines. For investors with a higher risk tolerance and the ability to withstand greater market fluctuations, Claude suggests a 60/40 split.

While Solana’s projected return slightly exceeds Bitcoin’s by 13 percentage points — 202.6% versus 189.8% — Claude notes that when factoring in probability-weighted expected returns, the outcomes appear more even. This is largely because Solana’s $70 price floor is lower than its current trading level.

Overall, we believe Bitcoin has a fair chance of reaching $240,000 by the end of 2030. Solana, on the other hand, faces more challenges in reaching the $320 target. For Bitcoin, achieving the goal depends on stabilizing corporate buying trends, boosting ETF flows, and surpassing its previous record of $126,080. For Solana, success hinges on the Alpenglow upgrade’s effectiveness and on becoming a go-to choice for stablecoin and tokenization projects.

Both forecasts carry a downside. If the corporate treasury trade unwinds, Claude’s $150,000 floor looks more realistic for Bitcoin, and if demand stays on Ethereum, Solana could drift toward $70. These predictions start from prices of about $82,810 for Bitcoin and $106 for Solana, where both coins traded when Claude made the forecast. This scenario also considers pressure from corporate treasuries, companies that borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin and could weigh on the market. The higher target assumes a strong post-halving rally and increased interest from institutional investors through exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Achieving the $240,000 target would represent a return of 189.8%, roughly 29% per year. As Bitcoin's supply is nearly capped at 21 million coins, with 20,098,843 already mined, any price increase will largely depend on new buyers entering the market. For Solana, the forecast is broader, ranging from $70 to $700. The $320 target represents a 202.6% return and is 9% above Solana's previous record. Unlike Bitcoin, Solana does not have a maximum supply, and its total supply of more than 636 million tokens already tops the 589 million in circulation. Hence, Solana would need to achieve a market value higher than its previous all-time high to reach this price point. Claude gives Bitcoin a 60% chance of reaching a new all-time high by the end of 2027, which would require a 52% gain from current levels. In contrast, Claude gives Solana a 30% chance of breaking its previous record, which would need a substantial 177% increase. Bitcoin's price predictions depend heavily on demand for Bitcoin ETFs, which directly hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. As of October 16, these ETFs held approximately $104.3 billion in net assets. However, investors have withdrawn a net total of $617.2 million from them in October through that date. For Claude's higher price forecast to materialize, this trend needs to reverse and turn into consistent buying. Bitcoin also faces risks, particularly from significant corporate treasury sales. For example, Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) holds about 848,250 BTC, or roughly 4% of the total supply, and new MSCI index rules could cost it billions in passive holdings by index funds. If MSCI excludes Strategy from its indexes starting November 30, demand for its shares could fall, potentially prompting Bitcoin selling as ETF demand wanes. For Solana to reach the high end of its forecast at $700, it must become the primary settlement layer for stablecoins (dollar-pegged tokens) and tokenized assets like stocks and bonds on the blockchain. The upcoming Alpenglow upgrade, scheduled for activation on October 21, aims to cut transaction finality, the point after which a transaction can't be reversed, to 150 milliseconds, which Claude says makes Solana's settlement pitch technically credible. However, the upgrade's success depends on network revenue growing with it. The main risk is that technological advancement could outpace demand if stablecoin issuers and tokenization projects continue to favor Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH). If given $5,000 to invest, Claude would allocate $3,500 to Bitcoin and $1,500 to Solana, balancing each investment based on potential price declines. For investors with a higher risk tolerance and the ability to withstand greater market fluctuations, Claude suggests a 60/40 split. While Solana's projected return slightly exceeds Bitcoin's by 13 percentage points — 202.6% versus 189.8% — Claude notes that when factoring in probability-weighted expected returns, the outcomes appear more even. This is largely because Solana's $70 price floor is lower than its current trading level. Overall, we believe Bitcoin has a fair chance of reaching $240,000 by the end of 2030. Solana, on the other hand, faces more challenges in reaching the $320 target. sources.title: How far can we push computing? - MIT Technology Review
passages: But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still.

Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space.
How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram?
In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.
Memory density obeys a limit of its own, and this one reaches all the way to gravity.

In 1981, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein, while working out the thermodynamics of black holes, determined the amount: The information inside any bounded region is limited by its size and the energy it contains.
For a region the size of Lloyd’s ultimate laptop, that comes to about 10 42 bits, some 10 36 to a cubic millimeter—nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size can store today.

extraction.body: Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing. MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands. The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale. Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace. Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling. SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed. Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. sources.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
passages: Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.
The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.
That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021.
The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.
“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.
The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch.
Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate.
Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even.
The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even.
The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.

The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers.
It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.
Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them.
Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.
“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

sources.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
passages: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents.
In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity.
Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.

sources.body: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. passages: If passed, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement.
Concerns around ownership, the ability to play, resell, or transfer games have drawn attention recently following Sony’s announcement that it planned to phase out physical game discs in 2028.

extraction.body: Ritchie Torres of New York’s 15th congressional district in the Bronx introduced the Power To The Players Act this week. If passed, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement. Meaning that when a company decides to shut down those servers, the games often become unplayable. 2K will be delisting the game from storefronts at the end of the month and shutting down its servers on December 31st, limiting its playability. Concerns around ownership, the ability to play, resell, or transfer games have drawn attention recently following Sony’s announcement that it planned to phase out physical game discs in 2028. Torres said, “A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.” The bill would not only give players ownership of a game, “rather than a license to play it,” but also require developers to institute an offline mode before shutting down supporting servers. That is similar to the Protect Our Games Act introduced by State Sen. John Kane in Pennsylvania, which would require companies to provide an offline gaming mode, an online gaming mode independent of the company’s servers, or a minimum 25 percent refund when titles are being sunset.

If passed, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement. Meaning that when a company decides to shut down those servers, the games often become unplayable. 2K will be delisting the game from storefronts at the end of the month and shutting down its servers on December 31st, limiting its playability. Concerns around ownership, the ability to play, resell, or transfer games have drawn attention recently following Sony’s announcement that it planned to phase out physical game discs in 2028. Torres said, “A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.” The bill would not only give players ownership of a game, “rather than a license to play it,” but also require developers to institute an offline mode before shutting down supporting servers. That is similar to the Protect Our Games Act introduced by State Sen. John Kane in Pennsylvania, which would require companies to provide an offline gaming mode, an online gaming mode independent of the company’s servers, or a minimum 25 percent refund when titles are being sunset.

extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase , the largest bank in the U.S., is doubling down on its bet on the crypto space by launching its own eponymous token, further blurring the lines between commercial banking and the crypto industry. The bank announced on Tuesday that it would be piloting the new digital currency called JPMD in the coming days, in partnership with crypto exchange Coinbase. Rather than a stablecoin , as some were expecting, JPMD will be a deposit token—a digital representation of a bank deposit that is managed with blockchain technology. The company filed a trademark for “JPMD” over the weekend. “This pilot combines the credibility of both JPMorgan and Base to help bring institutional money into a more global economy,” Jesse Pollack, VP of engineering at Coinbase, said in a statement. The token will be used to settle transfers around the clock and make cross-border business-to-business payments on Base, Naveen Mallela, global co-head of JPMorgan Chase’s blockchain division, Kinexys, told Fortune. “We have always believed in having a token-based solution on public blockchains,” he said. The bank plans to issue JPMD on Base, a public Ethereum -based blockchain managed by Coinbase . It will be exclusively available to JPMorgan’s institutional clients, which include corporations and pension funds, according to Mallela. However, JPMorgan plans to expand the use of its JPMD token to more institutional clients over the next few months. JPMorgan’s decision to create a deposit token instead of a stablecoin is a noteworthy break in an otherwise new corporate trend, and allows the bank to stand out in a crowded field. Several major companies including Meta and Google have recently expressed interest in incorporating stablecoins into their payment structures, likely because the cryptocurrency—which is backed 1:1 to the U.S. dollar—is considered more stable than other forms of crypto like Bitcoin . JPMorgan chose to launch a deposit token, rather than a stablecoin, because of its different use cases, Mallela said. Stablecoins, such as Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC, are primarily used by retail clients for crypto trading, remittances, and as a store of value, and are managed by crypto companies, he says. Deposit tokens, on the other hand, are more suitable for institutional clients because they are issued by a licensed bank, making them better integrated into existing institutional financial systems. “Institutional clients can treat JPMD as bank deposits on their balance sheet, providing certainty around financial and accounting treatment,” Mallela said. Each JPMD deposit token traded on Base will represent a deposit claim against JPMorgan. Rather than being backed 1:1 by the U.S. dollar like a stablecoin, JPMD will be backed by “the same liquidity frameworks as traditional banks,” Mallela said. Catherine McGrath is a crypto fellow at Fortune .

coreStoryFacts.text: BREAKING: JPMorgan Expands JPM Coin Deposit Token to Ethereum Network originally appeared on CoinGape
$5 trillion AUM JPMorgan Chase is launching its deposit token on Ethereum, extending the lender's push into blockchain payments as Wall Street grows more comfortable moving money on public networks.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The deposit token was first launched on Coinbase-linked blockchain Base last year.
As CoinGape reported, JPMorgan is expanding its Digital Assets and Blockchain Solutions team as it explores tokenized deposits, blockchain payments, digital assets and new products for consumers.
Morgan has now added a cash leg to the products it already live on Ethereum mainnet, with tokenized money market funds MONY and JLTXX both already on the network.

The token will be used to settle transfers around the clock and make cross-border business-to-business payments on Base, Naveen Mallela, global co-head of JPMorgan Chase’s blockchain division, Kinexys, told Fortune.
“We have always believed in having a token-based solution on public blockchains,” he said.
JPMorgan chose to launch a deposit token, rather than a stablecoin, because of its different use cases, Mallela said.
Deposit tokens, on the other hand, are more suitable for institutional clients because they are issued by a licensed bank, making them better integrated into existing institutional financial systems.
The bank plans to issue JPMD on Base, a public Ethereum -based blockchain managed by Coinbase .
It will be exclusively available to JPMorgan’s institutional clients, which include corporations and pension funds, according to Mallela.
However, JPMorgan plans to expand the use of its JPMD token to more institutional clients over the next few months.

JPMorgan Chase , the largest bank in the U.S., is doubling down on its bet on the crypto space by launching its own eponymous token, further blurring the lines between commercial banking and the crypto industry.
“This pilot combines the credibility of both JPMorgan and Base to help bring institutional money into a more global economy,” Jesse Pollack, VP of engineering at Coinbase, said in a statement.
“Institutional clients can treat JPMD as bank deposits on their balance sheet, providing certainty around financial and accounting treatment,” Mallela said.
Catherine McGrath is a crypto fellow at Fortune .
Landriault said JPMorgan chose Ethereum for its liquidity and existing use among clients.
While the tokens are issued on public networks, JPM Coin will remain restricted to approved institutional participants.
The expansion follows JPMorgan’s November 2025 rollout of JPM Coin on Base, an Ethereum layer-2 network built by cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase.
At the time, JPMorgan said it planned to support additional public blockchains.
In January, JPMorgan announced plans to bring JPM Coin to the Canton Network.
JPMorgan Chase, the world’s biggest bank by market capitalization, is expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, Bloomberg reported on Monday.
JPM Coin represents US dollar deposits held at JPMorgan and lets eligible clients transfer funds within seconds, around the clock.

extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase , the largest bank in the U.S., is doubling down on its bet on the crypto space by launching its own eponymous token, further blurring the lines between commercial banking and the crypto industry. The bank announced on Tuesday that it would be piloting the new digital currency called JPMD in the coming days, in partnership with crypto exchange Coinbase. Rather than a stablecoin , as some were expecting, JPMD will be a deposit token—a digital representation of a bank deposit that is managed with blockchain technology. The company filed a trademark for “JPMD” over the weekend. “This pilot combines the credibility of both JPMorgan and Base to help bring institutional money into a more global economy,” Jesse Pollack, VP of engineering at Coinbase, said in a statement. The token will be used to settle transfers around the clock and make cross-border business-to-business payments on Base, Naveen Mallela, global co-head of JPMorgan Chase’s blockchain division, Kinexys, told Fortune. “We have always believed in having a token-based solution on public blockchains,” he said. The bank plans to issue JPMD on Base, a public Ethereum -based blockchain managed by Coinbase . It will be exclusively available to JPMorgan’s institutional clients, which include corporations and pension funds, according to Mallela. However, JPMorgan plans to expand the use of its JPMD token to more institutional clients over the next few months. JPMorgan’s decision to create a deposit token instead of a stablecoin is a noteworthy break in an otherwise new corporate trend, and allows the bank to stand out in a crowded field. Several major companies including Meta and Google have recently expressed interest in incorporating stablecoins into their payment structures, likely because the cryptocurrency—which is backed 1:1 to the U.S. dollar—is considered more stable than other forms of crypto like Bitcoin . JPMorgan chose to launch a deposit token, rather than a stablecoin, because of its different use cases, Mallela said. Stablecoins, such as Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC, are primarily used by retail clients for crypto trading, remittances, and as a store of value, and are managed by crypto companies, he says. Deposit tokens, on the other hand, are more suitable for institutional clients because they are issued by a licensed bank, making them better integrated into existing institutional financial systems. “Institutional clients can treat JPMD as bank deposits on their balance sheet, providing certainty around financial and accounting treatment,” Mallela said. Each JPMD deposit token traded on Base will represent a deposit claim against JPMorgan. Rather than being backed 1:1 by the U.S. dollar like a stablecoin, JPMD will be backed by “the same liquidity frameworks as traditional banks,” Mallela said. Catherine McGrath is a crypto fellow at Fortune .

facts.text: BREAKING: JPMorgan Expands JPM Coin Deposit Token to Ethereum Network originally appeared on CoinGape
$5 trillion AUM JPMorgan Chase is launching its deposit token on Ethereum, extending the lender's push into blockchain payments as Wall Street grows more comfortable moving money on public networks.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The deposit token was first launched on Coinbase-linked blockchain Base last year.
As CoinGape reported, JPMorgan is expanding its Digital Assets and Blockchain Solutions team as it explores tokenized deposits, blockchain payments, digital assets and new products for consumers.
Morgan has now added a cash leg to the products it already live on Ethereum mainnet, with tokenized money market funds MONY and JLTXX both already on the network.

The token will be used to settle transfers around the clock and make cross-border business-to-business payments on Base, Naveen Mallela, global co-head of JPMorgan Chase’s blockchain division, Kinexys, told Fortune.
“We have always believed in having a token-based solution on public blockchains,” he said.
JPMorgan chose to launch a deposit token, rather than a stablecoin, because of its different use cases, Mallela said.
Deposit tokens, on the other hand, are more suitable for institutional clients because they are issued by a licensed bank, making them better integrated into existing institutional financial systems.
The bank plans to issue JPMD on Base, a public Ethereum -based blockchain managed by Coinbase .
It will be exclusively available to JPMorgan’s institutional clients, which include corporations and pension funds, according to Mallela.
However, JPMorgan plans to expand the use of its JPMD token to more institutional clients over the next few months.

JPMorgan Chase , the largest bank in the U.S., is doubling down on its bet on the crypto space by launching its own eponymous token, further blurring the lines between commercial banking and the crypto industry.
“This pilot combines the credibility of both JPMorgan and Base to help bring institutional money into a more global economy,” Jesse Pollack, VP of engineering at Coinbase, said in a statement.
“Institutional clients can treat JPMD as bank deposits on their balance sheet, providing certainty around financial and accounting treatment,” Mallela said.

While the tokens are issued on public networks, JPM Coin will remain restricted to approved institutional participants.

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » During downturns, I prefer companies with established competitive advantages , diversified revenue streams, and enough financial flexibility to keep investing while weaker competitors fall behind. This is why Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is near the top of my shopping list. One of Alphabet's biggest strengths is that so many of its products are embedded in everyday life. Think about how frequently people use Google Search, Gmail, YouTube, Google Maps, Android, and Chrome. Although the use of these services isn't a discretionary purchase in the traditional sense, they are integrated into how billions of people around the world communicate, navigate, work, and discover information. The advantage of this model is that Alphabet can attract users through its ecosystem of free services and monetize people's activity through advertising. Since its products are interconnected, Alphabet can easily introduce new features and services to existing customers rather than constantly creating new products and marketing to different demographics. Alphabet's reach extends far beyond consumers. Through Google Cloud, Alphabet provides computing infrastructure, cybersecurity, data analytics, and AI services to enterprise customers. This diversified business model comes in handy during economic downturns. Advertising budgets often decline when businesses become cautious, but enterprise technology budgets usually follow different priorities. The most compelling thing about Alphabet is the company's ability to vertically integrate its various businesses. Within Google Cloud, the company offers its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also operates data centers, builds AI models through Google DeepMind, and distributes AI-powered products through Search, Gemini, and Workspace. During the 2008 financial crisis, Alphabet shares declined 55% for the year. The recession pressured advertising spending, and investors abandoned growth stocks. The stock also experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of roughly 31% during the COVID-19 crash in early 2020. Most recently, Alphabet lost roughly 39% of its value during the 2022 bear market as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty dragged on the technology sector. While those are substantial losses, here's what makes Alphabet interesting. Despite experiencing multiple severe downturns, the company continued growing its businesses, launching new products, and quietly strengthening its competitive position. The gray-shaded columns in the chart below mark recessions. The theme here is that investors who bought Alphabet stock during market downturns and held on to their positions benefited materially from the company's subsequent recoveries. During the second quarter, Alphabet generated $119.8 billion in revenue, representing 24% growth year over year. Its Google Services segment generated $94.5 billion in revenue while Google Cloud grew an impressive 82% to $24.8 billion. This shows how Alphabet is able to benefit from both an established advertising franchise and the AI economy. The real story is that Alphabet generated $39.1 billion in operating cash flow during the second quarter, giving the company substantial financial resources to fund research, infrastructure, and other investments. The company ended June with $242.5 billion in cash and marketable securities. Alphabet's financial flexibility gives the company the ability to invest in AI infrastructure, develop new products, pursue acquisitions, and maintain shareholder distributions (i.e., dividends) without depending entirely on outside financing. Against this backdrop, Alphabet stock could still fall substantially if the market crashes. Nevertheless, history suggests the company's diversified ecosystem, vertical integration, and extraordinary financial horsepower put Alphabet in a good position to endure a downturn and emerge even stronger. Rather than attempting to time the next stock market crash, I'd consider buying Alphabet stock gradually over time during dips and holding it for the long term. Before you buy stock in Alphabet, consider this: The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Alphabet wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years. Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $380,363 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,315,732 !* Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 919% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 211% for the S&P 500. Don't miss the latest top 10 list, available with Stock Advisor , and join an investing community built by individual investors for individual investors. *Stock Advisor returns as of October 19, 2026. This translates into an annualized return of roughly 21% over four years, more than twice its historical average of approximately 10% annually, including dividends. Here's the catch: Stock prices do not outperform their long-term averages indefinitely. Eventually, markets experience mean reversion, a process in which unusually strong returns are followed by periods of weaker performance. While this doesn't guarantee a crash is imminent, one particular valuation indicator is flashing a warning investors should not ignore. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio (CAPE) measures the S&P 500's price relative to its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last 10 years. The point is to smooth out temporary earnings fluctuations, providing a more balanced perspective on whether stocks are expensive or fairly valued. Historically, the CAPE ratio has averaged around 17.8. But as of October 2026, readings are hovering around 41. To appreciate how unusual this is, consider some history. Before the 1929 stock market crash, the CAPE ratio approached 33. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES: ^DJI) subsequently lost 89% of its value between 1929 and 1932. In more recent history, the CAPE ratio exceeded 40 in 1999 and peaked near 44 before the dot-com bubble collapse. From March 2000 through October 2002, the S&P 500 declined 49%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) plunged 77%. Today's CAPE reading above 40 puts stock valuations in rare territory, suggesting the current market is historically expensive. Much like the internet revolution, generative AI promises to transform entire industries, leading investors to pay premiums for companies expected to dominate the future. But I see one important difference between today's AI boom and the dot-com bubble. During the late 1990s, investors poured unprecedented sums into speculative technology companies with little revenue, no profits, and untested business models. Today's AI leaders are considerably different. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) sells the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power much of the AI revolution. Despite its stock price appreciation over the last few years, Nvidia's earnings have also expanded as demand for its chips continues to accelerate. Meanwhile, Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) is benefiting from soaring demand for high bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM solutions. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) has combined an established, highly profitable advertising business with an expanding cloud infrastructure and AI services ecosystem. These businesses aren't selling investors a vision of the future. They're actually generating consistent AI-driven revenue and profits today. This is why their forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios look reasonable relative to what the broader market's CAPE ratio might suggest. The crack I see is that future growth in the AI landscape hinges on the overarching assumption that big tech will continue spending at historical levels on AI infrastructure. According to Morgan Stanley , capital expenditures (capex) among the five major hyperscalers -- Microsoft , Amazon , Alphabet, Meta Platforms , and Oracle -- are projected to approach $800 billion in 2026, climb to $1.2 trillion in 2027, and reach $1.4 trillion in 2028. Those investments are an enormous opportunity for Nvidia, Micron, and other semiconductor suppliers. But they also create a financial opportunity cost. Every dollar AI hyperscalers spend building data centers is one that cannot also be used to fund share repurchases or dividend increases. If AI infrastructure investments fail to deliver attractive returns on aggressive timelines, Wall Street could eventually question whether these budgets were justified. The combination of outsize gains over the last four years fueling historically elevated valuations suggests the market has less room for disappointment. This is why taking some profits right now could make sense. In particular, for investors whose portfolios have become heavily concentrated in AI-related technology stocks, trimming some of your biggest winners could prove wise. Of course, selling everything would be a questionable decision. Instead, I'd consider maintaining exposure to AI through a more diversified cohort of businesses. Industrial companies stand to benefit from data center construction, electrical equipment, and automation, while energy companies can profit from rising demand for electricity and natural gas. Meanwhile, utilities should benefit from investments in power generation and transmission infrastructure. The biggest mistake investors can make right now is assuming that historically expensive valuations mean a crash is right around the corner. During the 2008 financial crisis, Alphabet shares declined 55% for the year. The recession pressured advertising spending, and investors abandoned growth stocks. The stock also experienced a peak-to-trough drawdown of roughly 31% during the COVID-19 crash in early 2020. Most recently, Alphabet lost roughly 39% of its value during the 2022 bear market as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty dragged on the technology sector.

While those are substantial losses, here's what makes Alphabet interesting. Despite experiencing multiple severe downturns, the company continued growing its businesses, launching new products, and quietly strengthening its competitive position. The gray-shaded columns in the chart below mark recessions. The theme here is that investors who bought Alphabet stock during market downturns and held on to their positions benefited materially from the company's subsequent recoveries.

During the second quarter, Alphabet generated $119.8 billion in revenue, representing 24% growth year over year. Its Google Services segment generated $94.5 billion in revenue while Google Cloud grew an impressive 82% to $24.8 billion. This shows how Alphabet is able to benefit from both an established advertising franchise and the AI economy.

The real story is that Alphabet generated $39.1 billion in operating cash flow during the second quarter, giving the company substantial financial resources to fund research, infrastructure, and other investments. The company ended June with $242.5 billion in cash and marketable securities.

Alphabet's financial flexibility gives the company the ability to invest in AI infrastructure, develop new products, pursue acquisitions, and maintain shareholder distributions (i.e., dividends) without depending entirely on outside financing.

Against this backdrop, Alphabet stock could still fall substantially if the market crashes. Nevertheless, history suggests the company's diversified ecosystem, vertical integration, and extraordinary financial horsepower put Alphabet in a good position to endure a downturn and emerge even stronger. Rather than attempting to time the next stock market crash , I'd consider buying Alphabet stock gradually over time during dips and holding it for the long term.
