extraction.body: Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing. MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace. Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling. SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed. Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits. Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate. These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop. The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc 2 , holds about 9 ×10 16 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×10 50 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today. The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop. Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10 -21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch. Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun. The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter. Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation. Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined. But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in. This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat. Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication. Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet. It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter. But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.

sources.title: DARPA plans ‘major expansion’ of quantum computing push next month - Breaking Defense
passages: WASHINGTON — The self-proclaimed “quantum skeptic” heading DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) tells Breaking Defense he is “pleasantly surprised” by how many companies’ quantum computing plans look feasible — and as a result, he’s weeks away from announcing a slew of new awards.
“A year from now we’ll know a lot more about if this industry is for real or not.”
At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said.

Currently, it consists of roughly 200 quantum experts from across the government — including Energy Department labs like Los Alamos as well as Defense Department labs like the Air Force Research Laboratory — and government-funded research centers, such as Johns Hopkins. (These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work).
The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way.
“That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C.
“We are building by far the best, largest test and evaluation team for quantum computing on the planet,” Altepeter summed up. “[We’re] planning for this to be a $1 billion-plus program.”

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers.

sources.title: The world needs ever faster data processing. Edge computing will help - Mastercard
passages: The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever.
Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate.
Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data.
The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection.
This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through.

For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves.
That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again.
The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second.
For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world.
In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols.
Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately.
Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center.

Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes.
The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds.
Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers.
The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones.
As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage.
Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster.
And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously.
It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway.
Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions.
There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations.
Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

coreStoryFacts.text: But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still.

Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space.
How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram?
In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.

(These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work).
The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way.
“That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C.

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers.
The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever.
Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate.
Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data.
The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection.
This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through.

For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves.
That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again.
The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second.
For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world.
In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols.
Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately.
Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center.

Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes.
The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds.
Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers.
The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones.
As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage.
Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster.
And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously.
It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway.
Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions.
There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations.
Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

extraction.body: Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing. MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace. Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling. SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed. Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits. Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate. These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop. The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc 2 , holds about 9 ×10 16 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×10 50 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today. The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop. Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10 -21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch. Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun. The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter. Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation. Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined. But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in. This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat. Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication. Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet. It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter. But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
passages: Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing.
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here .

On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.

In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out.

The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.

But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains.

Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.

Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.

Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling.
SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS

For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed.

Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits.

Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate.

These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.

The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc 2 , holds about 9 ×10 16 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×10 50 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today.

The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop.

Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10 -21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch.

Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun.

The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter.

Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation.

Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined.

But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in.

This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat.

Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication.

Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet.

It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter.

But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.

sources.title: DARPA plans ‘major expansion’ of quantum computing push next month - Breaking Defense
passages: WASHINGTON — The self-proclaimed “quantum skeptic” heading DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) tells Breaking Defense he is “pleasantly surprised” by how many companies’ quantum computing plans look feasible — and as a result, he’s weeks away from announcing a slew of new awards.
“A year from now we’ll know a lot more about if this industry is for real or not.”
At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said.

Currently, it consists of roughly 200 quantum experts from across the government — including Energy Department labs like Los Alamos as well as Defense Department labs like the Air Force Research Laboratory — and government-funded research centers, such as Johns Hopkins. (These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work).
The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way.
“That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C.
“We are building by far the best, largest test and evaluation team for quantum computing on the planet,” Altepeter summed up. “[We’re] planning for this to be a $1 billion-plus program.”

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers.

The point of the QBI program is not to pay the private sector to develop the tech, which they’re already doing on their own, according to program manager Joe Altepeter. Instead, in essence, a company that wins a QBI award gets access to DARPA’s interagency team of expert testers and devil’s advocates, serving as an independent outside check to make sure that they’re on a practical path. Tech titan Microsoft and specialist startup PsiQuantum have already won contracts for the initial, pilot-project version of the program, known clunkily as Underexplored Systems for Utility-Scale Quantum Computing or US2QC . (“You can tell why we changed it to ‘QBI,’” Altepeter said). Two other companies, Atom Computing and QC82 , also won preliminary, short-term grants in 2023, but their proposals didn’t survive subsequent rounds of more intensive scrutiny. So only two of four competing firms made it all the way through the three-phase process to win one of the long-term “Stage C” contracts announced Feb. 6. That 50 percent success rate is actually much better than Altepeter expected. “That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C. But that’s why we do this, to get surprised.” So a “major expansion” to “bring in many more companies” is now underway, Altepeter said. “We’ve gotten finished with source selection [and] sent out letters inviting all the companies who’ve made it into stage A to negotiate a contract…. My best guess is late March, we’re going to have the vast majority of those contracts signed.” In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers. As a result, “we’ll have the chance to kick the tires on a lot more companies,” he said. “A year from now, we’ll know a lot more about if this industry is for real or not.” How does that timeline work? The process is meant to be flexible, with the schedule accommodating what companies think is required, and companies that fail at one stage of the evaluation — like Atom and QC82 — are welcome to come back for a second shot. But overall, Altepeter said, QBI goes like this: At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said. Currently, it consists of roughly 200 quantum experts from across the government — including Energy Department labs like Los Alamos as well as Defense Department labs like the Air Force Research Laboratory — and government-funded research centers, such as Johns Hopkins. (These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work). The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way. With new technologies, it’s all too easy to get sucked in by hype cycles and impressive statistics, Altepeter said, so it’s critical, and difficult, to figure out the right way to measure progress. Track the wrong metrics, he warned, and you end up with the equivalent of assessing a space-launch program by highest altitude achieved to date, a superficially reasonable approach that ends up grading grifters who can climb a ladder over professionals conducting static rocket-motor tests. “We are building by far the best, largest test and evaluation team for quantum computing on the planet,” Altepeter summed up. “[We’re] planning for this to be a $1 billion-plus program.” This kind of careful evaluation isn’t cheap, he acknowledged, and if too many companies prove qualified, he may not have enough funding to give all of them awards. “It’s a double-edged sword,” Altepeter said. “I’m pleasantly surprised that these companies were doing so well. I also worry that we couldn’t eliminate as many companies, because we’re definitely trying to eliminate companies.” Could the Trump Administration’s controversial ongoing cuts to government agencies, spearheaded by Elon Musk’s DOGE , cramp or cripple the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative just as it’s trying to grow? Altepeter demurred on those “bigger-scope…budget issues.” That said, when it comes to federal funding, “it’s always a danger that there are other priorities that take precedence,” he said. “But my marching orders are the same as they have been since we started this…which is to sprint as fast as possible and get ready for a world-changing program.”

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers. At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said. sources.title: The world needs ever faster data processing. Edge computing will help - Mastercard
passages: The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever.
Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate.
Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data.
The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection.
This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through.

For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves.
That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again.
The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second.
For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world.
In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols.
Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately.
Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center.

Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes.
The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds.
Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers.
The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones.
As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage.
Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster.
And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously.
It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway.
Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions.
There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations.
Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

extraction.body: Few innovations have transformed our relationship with technology like the cloud. This constellation of huge data centers can tackle computing tasks for digital devices located a mile or a continent away, allowing us to enjoy podcasts, share memes or stream movies nearly anywhere we go. The cloud, however, has a problem. It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway. That means more and more data and computing is being shuttled back and forth across the cloud’s connections, and more is coming. Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions. There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations. Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center. Edge computing isn’t new. Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes. Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers. The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones. For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world. In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols. Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately. Those days are over. As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage. Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster. The solution is to constantly evolve the network to make the edge do more work. Mastercard’s global network, for example, processes tens of billions of transactions a year, linking merchants, banks, government agencies, fintechs and open banking networks. The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection. This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through. Public cloud and 5G have increased consumer expectations for speed in our digital interactions, but they also allow for a range of innovations. For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves. That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again. The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second. Any longer and lines would start to stretch. There are applications, though, with even lower tolerances for lag. Congestion pricing is being used by more cities as a way to discourage drivers from bringing their vehicles into city centers during rush hour. And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously. The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever. Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate. Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data. Someday soon, we won’t just use our phones or wallets for commerce. Cars and kitchen appliances will play a role, too — recommending when it’s time for new tires, an oil change or a gallon of milk. Managing all that data and creating a unified experience across all of these devices will be a huge challenge. Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

story.title: How far can we push computing?

facts.text: But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still.

Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space.
How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram?
In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.

WASHINGTON — The self-proclaimed “quantum skeptic” heading DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) tells Breaking Defense he is “pleasantly surprised” by how many companies’ quantum computing plans look feasible — and as a result, he’s weeks away from announcing a slew of new awards.
“A year from now we’ll know a lot more about if this industry is for real or not.”
At each stage, the size and cost of the DARPA team roughly doubles, Altepeter said.

Currently, it consists of roughly 200 quantum experts from across the government — including Energy Department labs like Los Alamos as well as Defense Department labs like the Air Force Research Laboratory — and government-funded research centers, such as Johns Hopkins. (These personnel will remain with their home organization but spend roughly 60 to 70 percent of their time on DARPA quantum work).
The idea, he said, is to get independent, expert feedback from professionals with no financial stake in the outcome either way.
“That was definitely surprising,” he told Breaking Defense. “I didn’t think anybody was going to make it to Stage C.
“We are building by far the best, largest test and evaluation team for quantum computing on the planet,” Altepeter summed up. “[We’re] planning for this to be a $1 billion-plus program.”

In this new round of competition, once again, Altepeter said many competitors exceeded his expectations for how far along their tech is and how feasible their plans are to build reliable, practical, and usefully powerful quantum computers.

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has become a major beneficiary of rising demand for memory chips, which has fueled record revenue and earnings growth over the last year. What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory. If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY). Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models . As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market. One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate. Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers. SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems. Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic are all developing custom silicon chips. This provides yet another tailwind for increased memory demand and could help SK Hynix diversify across different AI computing architectures. In other words, SK Hynix doesn't need one chip designer to dominate the AI infrastructure era indefinitely. It simply needs advanced memory to remain essential to the broader AI ecosystem. While AI-driven growth has fueled substantial earnings expansion for SK Hynix, the company's valuation remains fairly modest on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis. The company's leadership in the HBM market and progress in new chip technology give SK Hynix strong competitive advantages that extend beyond today's memory supercycle. When combined with its attractive valuation profile, I view SK Hynix as a compelling long-term buy for investors seeking exposure to the AI infrastructure boom. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $2,783,470 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. *Stock Advisor returns as of October 18, 2026. extraction.body: Micron Technology ( MU -5.63% ) has become a major beneficiary of rising demand for memory chips, which has fueled record revenue and earnings growth over the last year. What investors may not fully understand is that Micron isn't the only company poised to capitalize on artificial intelligence's insatiable appetite for memory. If I could own just one AI memory stock for the next five years, my choice would be SK Hynix ( SKHY -6.58% ) . Let's dig into why I think SK Hynix stock deserves a closer look. Most investors think of Nvidia and its graphics processing units (GPUs) when they think about AI. These processors wouldn't be nearly as effective without high bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM allows AI accelerators to access large quantities of information quickly, making it a critical input for training generative AI models . As Nvidia and other semiconductor designers develop more powerful chip architectures, the memory accompanying these chips needs to be faster, more efficient, and capable of handling larger workloads. This is where SK Hynix stands out. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix accounted for 50% of global HBM revenue as of the second quarter, nearly as much as Samsung and Micron combined. SK Hynix achieved its market leadership through early investments in advanced memory packaging and manufacturing technologies, giving it a first-mover advantage in the HBM market. One of the biggest risks facing memory manufacturers is the industry's cyclical boom-and-bust cycle. When demand accelerates, manufacturers expand production. Naturally, supply catches up, prices fall, and profit margins deteriorate. Advanced AI memory introduces an interesting nuance. The companies designing next-generation AI accelerators need memory suppliers capable of meeting increasingly demanding technical requirements. In turn, this encourages close collaboration between semiconductor designers like Nvidia and memory producers. SK Hynix is positioned particularly well for this transition. The company began mass shipments of HBM4 during the second quarter, while continuing development of its next-generation HBM4E products. These developments should strengthen its relationships with customers building more powerful accelerated computing systems. Interestingly, SK Hynix's opportunities extend beyond Nvidia's GPUs. AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Anthropic are all developing custom silicon chips . This provides yet another tailwind for increased memory demand and could help SK Hynix diversify across different AI computing architectures. In other words, SK Hynix doesn't need one chip designer to dominate the AI infrastructure era indefinitely. It simply needs advanced memory to remain essential to the broader AI ecosystem. While AI-driven growth has fueled substantial earnings expansion for SK Hynix, the company's valuation remains fairly modest on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis. The company's leadership in the HBM market and progress in new chip technology give SK Hynix strong competitive advantages that extend beyond today's memory supercycle. When combined with its attractive valuation profile, I view SK Hynix as a compelling long-term buy for investors seeking exposure to the AI infrastructure boom . Shares of Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) have more than tripled so far in 2026. Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) has delivered an even greater return, with its stock up close to 6X year to date.

But, as the fund disclosures say, past performance isn't necessarily indicative of future results. Which of these two AI memory stocks is the better pick to own over the next three years? Here's how Micron and Sandisk stack up against each other.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Historically, Micron has been a cyclical stock with wild price swings. Its shares are still highly volatile, but the price swings have primarily been in one direction -- up.

There's a simple reason why that's the case. Demand for memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM), has gone through the roof so much that Micron and other manufacturers can't create enough supply to keep up.

Don't expect these dynamics to change anytime soon. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said in his company's fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings call in June, "We expect tight conditions to persist beyond calendar 2027 as a result of AI-driven demand across all segments coupled with structural supply constraints."

The segments Mehrotra referred to include cloud memory, core data center, mobile and client, and automotive and embedded. Micron makes DRAM, HBM (which uses DRAM as a component), and NAND memory chips -- and all are enjoying strong demand.

What if the AI data center boom loses fizz? Micron expects another strong tailwind from humanoid robots. Mehrotra predicts that this nascent market will have a "sustained, substantial multi-decade memory demand cycle."

Sandisk's 2026 performance is impressive, making it the biggest winner by far in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) . What's even more stunning is that the memory stock has skyrocketed roughly 3900% since it was spun off from Western Digital (NASDAQ: WDC) in February 2025.

Like Micron, Sandisk is riding the wave of a massive supply demand imbalance. AI data centers are gobbling up every bit of NAND memory they can get. That's because NAND flash has become the most cost-effective solution for large-scale AI inference (applying trained AI models to analyze real data).

Can this momentum last? Sandisk CEO David Goeckeler thinks so. He told analysts in the company's April 2026 earnings call that Sandisk now has "a durable growth model, a valuable franchise, and a business built to generate substantial, sustained cash flow."

Wall Street believes Sandisk has plenty of room to run. The consensus 12-month price target reflects an upside of over 50%. Of the 23 analysts surveyed by S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI) in August, 18 rated the stock as a "buy" or "strong buy."
I expect both of these AI memory stocks to deliver market-beating returns over the next three years. However, if I had to pick only one to own, I think the nod goes to Micron.

For one thing, Micron has a more diversified business than Sandisk. If demand for one type of memory slows, Micron could continue to grow. Size matters, too. Micron is roughly five times larger than Sandisk and ranks as the world's third-largest memory chip manufacturer by revenue .

Valuation is another consideration. Sandisk isn't expensive, with shares trading at below 19 times forward earnings. But Micron looks like a steal with a forward earnings multiple of only 5.3. The stock's price-to-earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio, which is based on analysts' five-year earnings growth projections, is also an absurdly low 0.12.
Granted, if data center demand slows significantly, both of these stocks will be hit hard. I don't envision that happening over the next three years.

Micron makes DRAM, HBM (which uses DRAM as a component), and NAND memory chips -- and all are enjoying strong demand.
Historically, Micron has been a cyclical stock with wild price swings.
Its shares are still highly volatile, but the price swings have primarily been in one direction -- up.
